Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (242 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, LONDON — In Paris, in the years leading up to the massive social upheavals of 1968, Julio Le Parc was making the first of his Game Rooms.
  • A recreation of one of the Game Rooms appears in the exhibition Julio Le Parc: Light.

According to recent reports, LONDON — In Paris, in the years leading up to the massive social upheavals of 1968, Julio Le Parc was making the first of his Game Rooms. These were collections of works that aimed to playfully destabilize the viewer’s experience, such as seats with springs that challenged the act of sitting, areas of uneven tile floors, and patterned discs designed to be manually spun. But for Le Parc, as well as the progressive collective Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV) that he co-founded, the works were about far more than entertainment. Indeed, he hoped that cultivating the audience’s active participation would not only disrupt what he saw as the hierarchical and passive nature of the museum, but also effect a political awakening outside of it.

A recreation of one of the Game Rooms appears in the exhibition Julio Le Parc: Light. Colour. Action., which was “developed in close dialogue with the artist,” before his death earlier this year at the age of 97. Though the current world, as in 1960s Paris, grapples with mounting social and political tensions, one is unlikely to describe today’s art museum experience as “passive.” Indeed, outgoing Tate Modern Interim Director Catherine Wood notes in the exhibition catalog’s foreword, “At a time of heightened popularity for exhibitions touting immersive and interactive experiences, celebrating Julio Le Parc’s seven-decade career with a monographic exhibition at Tate Modern feels especially meaningful and urgent.”.

Latest Update: South London Gallery director Margot Heller to leave role after 25 years

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years.
  • Recent findings suggest that heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser.
  • “After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for new adventures in my career,” Heller said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years. Over this time the institution’s physical footprint has more than tripled and visitor numbers increased tenfold, according to a gallery statement.

Recent findings suggest that heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser. She will retain a connection with the gallery, curating the Dutch artist’s Mark Manders’s first solo exhibition at a London institution, opening at SLG on 23 September 2027.

“After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for new adventures in my career,” Heller said in a statement.

In a recent development, “From the day I took up the role, I saw an opportunity to build an institution that could be internationally acclaimed for its contemporary art programme, and deeply embedded in its local community. I have stayed true to that vision ever since.”.

Serge Ramin, the chair of the gallery’s trustees, described Heller as “a visionary curator and cultural leader”, adding: “She leaves a museum that is artistically ambitious, rooted in its community and physically transformed.”.

Heller’s tenure encompassed two major building projects with 6a architects: the conversion of a neighbouring house and construction of an education studio in 2010, followed by the opening of the former Peckham Road Fire Station in 2018.

The fire station was donated in 2014 by the artist Raqib Shaw, whose identity was initially withheld. Its conversion cost £4m. Heller told The Art Newspaper in 2018 that the gallery had not been actively seeking to expand when the building was offered.

A garden designed by Gabriel Orozco opened in 2016, while Art Block, the gallery’s free space for children and young people on the neighbouring Sceaux Gardens estate, opened at its current site in 2017.

The artist and SLG trustee Alvaro Barrington remarked: “In Margot’s time at the South London Gallery she has created pivotal moments in many artists’ careers, including my own.”.

He added: “Her commissioning of the Orozco Garden should be considered one of the most important architectural interventions in the UK.”.

Sources indicate that exhibitions Heller has worked on during her tenure include solo presentations by Steve McQueen, Rashid Johnson, Oscar Murillo, Michael Armitage and Christina Quarles. The gallery was a joint winner of Art Fund’s Museum of the Year award in 2020.

According to recent reports, before joining the SLG, Heller worked at Southampton City Art Gallery, becoming its director, and as director of exhibitions at Anthony d’Offay Gallery. She was appointed OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) in 2014.

The gallery became an independent charity in 2003, having previously been managed by Southwark Council.

Joy Gregory, an artist and SLG trustee, noted of Heller in a statement: “As a local resident and artist, I am enormously grateful for the extraordinary legacy she leaves behind and excited to see what she does next.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Mighty Miniatures,” an exhibition celebrating the intricate art of miniatures, is on view at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian in Newly introduced York from Saturday, November 21 through Friday, August 20, 2027. Curated by Anya Montiel (Tohono O’odham descent), the exhibition features over 300 pieces of art that showcase the skill of Indigenous weavers, sculptors, carvers and other artists that work on a miniscule scale.

The exhibition includes tiny masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries by artists from Indigenous communities from North and South America, as well as Hawai'i and the Caribbean. The small works reflect worldviews and cultural expressions, encouraging play and transferring intergenerational knowledge.

In a recent development, “‘Mighty Miniatures’ brings together some of the smallest works in the museum collection, reaching across the Western Hemisphere and spanning nearly 200 years,” Montiel mentioned. “It is amazing to see how these miniatures have been made with such skill, ingenuity, and detail. This exhibition is a celebration of Indigenous artistry on a small scale and the artists who create them.”.

In a recent development, left: Nahua doll’s chair, no date. Wood, yarn. 0.7 x 0.5 in. (14/4064); right: Tohono O’odham I’itoi ki: (Man-in-the-Maze) miniature basket, ca. 2000. Arizona. Horsehair. 4 x 2.6 in. 26/8865.

The exhibition is divided into six sections:.

Left: Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) canoe model, no date. Minnesota, Birchbark, sinew, paint. 0.5 x 2.4 x 1.1 in. (20/4941); right: Floyd Kingeekuk Sr. (Siberian Yupik, 1933–2006), ringed seal figure, 1975. Savoonga, Alaska. Ivory, ink. 0.9 x 4.1 x 1.2 in. (27/684).

It has been revealed that A family-friendly opening program is scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12, 11 AM–4 PM. Multi-disciplinary artist Lance Cardinal (Cree), a finalist on the TV show Best In Miniature, will lead visitors in mini drum making sessions. Gallery tours by Montiel will illuminate the stories behind the objects and discuss how the exhibition came together.

Strategy your visit at AmericanIndian.si.edu.

Tech Report: Tonkin Liu creates pair of glulam buildings for craftspeople restoring York Minster

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (561 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • London architecture studio Tonkin Liu has created two timber buildings on either side of York Minster, which contain facilities for workers restoring the Gothic cathedral.
  • Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stone masons views of the Grade I-listed York Minster.
  • “These are the first two buildings to be built with historical precedent in a hundred years; it was notable that they responded to the setting and heralded a latest chapter for heritage craft,” Tonkin Liu co-founder Mike Tonkin told Dezeen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by David Valinsky.

London architecture studio Tonkin Liu has created two timber buildings on either side of York Minster, which contain facilities for workers restoring the Gothic cathedral.

Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stone masons views of the Grade I-listed York Minster.

“These are the first two buildings to be built with historical precedent in a hundred years; it was notable that they responded to the setting and heralded a latest chapter for heritage craft,” Tonkin Liu co-founder Mike Tonkin told Dezeen.

In a recent development, “The restoration of York Minster needed to be accelerated because climate change is increasing its degradation,” he continued. “The two fresh buildings will speed up the conservation by four decades within the next century.”.

Working with preservation body Historic England and local planning authorities, Tonkin Liu retained, repurposed and extended a series of existing structures near York’s medieval city walls to form the Heritage Quad.

Its facilities, which contain workshops and education spaces for stonemasons and accommodation for apprentices, are united by glued-laminated timber (glulam) and a plywood roof that extends to partially cover a central courtyard.

Its distinctive roof channels water into rainwater tanks, rounding over the courtyard to give working masons a framed view of York Minster, and tilting up at the northern end to give passersby views into the workshops.

On the other side of the cathedral, the steel-and-glulam-constructed Technology Hub houses digital technology tools for stone cutting.

Triangular in plan, the hub features rows of arched windows rising from its photovoltaic-covered roof.

“Planning restricted the upper height within the surrounding buildings, and cutting equipment and gantry cranes set the lower structural height limit,” said Tonkin.

“The need to allow views of the Minster and light into the surrounding buildings led to parabolic fan vaults that fill the workshop with light.”.

Both the Heritage Quad and the Technology Hub were constructed from glulam, setting them apart from their historic neighbour.

“The buildings are fabricated in timber – stone is reserved for the Minster,” remarked Tonkin.

However, Tonkin Liu drew upon the cathedral’s use of light and geometry when designing two structures.

“The two buildings work within the ecclesiastical tradition that celebrates structure, geometry and light,” said Tonkin. “Both buildings have a physical and symbolic relationship to the Minster.”.

“The roof of Heritage Quad rises between the square and the circle, forming an arch that gives the masons a clear view of the Minster – the verticality of the expressed structure works with the tradition of the Minster’s perpendicular Gothic character,” he continued.

“The Technology Hub’s triangular strategy is set back from the boundary wall to maintain views of the Minster from the surrounding houses,” added Tonkin. “The wooden vaults find strength through form, as in the Minster, and trusses align with the existing walls and consequently radiate towards the transept of the Minster.”.

The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills is shortlisted in the mixed-use category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects completed by Tonkin Liu that have featured on Dezeen include a biometric tower in Manchester’s Civic Quarter and a swing bridge at London’s Crystal Palace Park, which gives access to an island filled with 19th-century concrete dinosaur models.

Photography by David Valinsky.

#22283. I trusted Adobe Firefly because it was the safe AI option, now I'm not so sure

📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq ↗ Open Full Page

I trusted Adobe Firefly because it was the safe AI option, now I'm not so sure

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adobe spent years selling Firefly on one massive reassurance: it was trained on licensed and public-domain content, so you didn't have to worry about where the pixels came from.
  • But I'd like to know what "commercially safe" covers once you've picked someone else's model.
  • There's an vital distinction here, too: Adobe's commercial-use assurances for its own Firefly models shouldn't be taken as a blanket guarantee for everything generated inside Firefly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adobe spent years selling Firefly on one massive reassurance: it was trained on licensed and public-domain content, so you didn't have to worry about where the pixels came from. While other AI companies faced accusations of scraping first and asking questions later, Adobe didn't, and made sure we knew about it. I like that about Firefly and Adobe's push for labelling and clarity, but things are changing.At MAX this week, Firefly got some noisy neighbours. Models from ByteDance, Google, Kling, OpenAI and ElevenLabs now sit alongside Firefly, with Adobe's Creative Agent in the same place. The keynote line was that creators get to choose, which sounds like a way of passing the buck onto us, the users.

According to recent reports, fine. But I'd like to know what "commercially safe" covers once you've picked someone else's model. The clean-data claim was about Firefly, and I guess it still is, but Firefly now sits alongside less open AI models. Adobe's position with Firefly was never a claim about OpenAI's training set or ByteDance's. A designer or artist clicking through the options could be forgiven for assuming the Adobe badge applies to everything inside the Adobe app. Adobe spells out the distinction in its partner-model documentation, but I'd argue this needs to be much clearer at the point of generation, not buried in the small print.

There's an vital distinction here, too: Adobe's commercial-use assurances for its own Firefly models shouldn't be taken as a blanket guarantee for everything generated inside Firefly. Partner models have their own terms, training histories and conditions of use, and users need to assess those separately. For agencies and studios, that difference matters. A Firefly badge isn't necessarily the same as a Firefly guarantee.

According to recent reports, even before opening its gated community to other AI models, Adobe came under pressure from people uploading AI versions of other artists' work and claiming them as Adobe Stock, so some bad actors found ways around Adobe's walled garden. Adobe took action and says it respects creators' rights, and that resemblance isn't proof of copying.Still, the complaints point at something licensing can't settle. Licensed training data answers whether Adobe was allowed to use the images. Artists were asking whether the output leans on their look. Those are separate questions, and the marketing has tended to let the first stand in for the second.Add other companies' models and the problem grows. 'Safe' stops describing the product and starts describing one entry on a list. Agencies and art directors who signed off on Firefly because of that word now have to check each model separately, and I suspect most won't. It's this idea that we, the people, the artists and designers, are now responsible for ensuring Firefly outputs are as ethical as they can be.

What I'd want from Adobe is, frankly, very dull and specific. Say in plain language, next to each model, what it was trained on. Say what the safe label does and doesn't cover, style included. Make it easy for studios to lock their workspaces to Firefly models alone, and make those controls available to everyone who needs them.Adobe has earned a fairly good reputation for adopting AI carefully and responsibly in AI's gold-rush free-for-all. It can keep that and run a marketplace, but only by showing which parts of the marketplace are ethical, carefully made and sourced.

To see what's likely coming down the line, read our report on the Adobe Sneaks from Max 2026, including one in particular that caught the eye: Project Link Up, which is set to make vector design more accessible.

Industry observers note that ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian debuted Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Tommaso Riva.

Australian studio YSG has converted a former private vacation residence into a boutique hotel in Bali focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture.

The Moon Gang Bali hotel is located among the rice fields on the northern outskirts of Ubud and includes five interconnected suites, outdoor terraces and a lounge surrounding a central courtyard.

According to its Australian hoteliers, the hotel was inspired by “our feverish obsession with Indonesian music and culture” and its offerings include an all-day spa and a “DIY DJ station” stacked with Indonesian and Japanese city pop records curated by DJ Midnight Runners.

YSG was similarly influenced by Indonesian and Japanese design for the hotel’s spaces, which feature bamboo and timber structures and lava stone tiling.

“Once a private vacation residence in severe disrepair, the concrete bunker was radically transformed into a modern-day Babylon infused with cosmic references and hybrid Japanese architectural elements, including the spa’s sliding bamboo doors depicting lunar phases,” the studio said.

The hotel is only accessible via motorbike or on foot, according to the team, and is located along an alleyway.

Guests enter on the far side of the courtyard pool, while the suites and common areas enclose the space on three sides.

The suites were designed with “dreamers, misfits and wanderers in mind”, according to the hotel, and each is outfitted with an assortment of objects by local studios set against walls clad in recycled earth-based finishes.

Locally made objects throughout the hotel include counter and stools manufactured from recycled plastic bottle tops by Weedoo Plastics, pool lounge chairs handwoven from upcycled materials by BYO Living and wall sconces made of local seseh wood and green-coloured resin by AA Practice.

YSG also made efforts to source construction materials locally while working on the project, as the studio noted it was difficult to transport them to the secluded site.

This included crushing terracotta tiles and breeze blocks and repurposing them as flooding riffraff to help with drainage, and joinery designed to be assembled on site.

The studio also addressed significant water damage to the complex and replaced rotten wooden walls, portions of the roof and concrete flooring.

The project also included adding a second-storey suite made of bamboo with an oversized skylight.

Other details include a black-and-white checkered tile relief that surrounds the pool’s edge, as a nod to the Saput Poleng cloths wrapped around holy objects as part of local customs.

YSG previously converted a warehouse into a co-working space in Sydney and brought 1970s elements to a local cafe.

Photography by Tommaso Riva.

Tech Report: Martin Puryear’s Liberatory Violence

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (240 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ATLANTA — Despite my best efforts to be anything else, I am a writer, and not even the Marines-like insanity of Bard’s interdisciplinary MFA or my day job in the library could erase that from me.
  • Recent findings suggest that I was grateful for that compulsion, however, when I viewed Martin Puryear’s Nexus.

ATLANTA — Despite my best efforts to be anything else, I am a writer, and not even the Marines-like insanity of Bard’s interdisciplinary MFA or my day job in the library could erase that from me. Every object instantly becomes a word I see on a perfectly white page, a symbol made up of assorted shapes like “bicycle” (object that carried me from my home to the High Museum of Art) or “press pass” (object that allows me into the High Museum of Art), a compulsion that is always at its worst when viewing sculpture in the page-white tomb of a museum.

Recent findings suggest that I was grateful for that compulsion, however, when I viewed Martin Puryear’s Nexus. Writing, underneath its surface, is extremely violent, exceptionally bloody, and annihilatory in scope. It is almost impossible to describe the reality of this fact on the page, and I have struggled even further to articulate this vocally to others, even other writers. So when walking into Nexus and “Bask” (1976) was there, lying as still and deadly as a knife on its white plinth, I smiled in surprised relief and my body physically relaxed. Puryear is noted for his use of natural materials — wood, rawhide, fiber — and his attention to traditional practices like basket weaving, boatmaking, tanning, and structure building from peoples around the world, which obscures the sculptures’ violence under that tricky word, “natural.”.

These days, Frida Kahlo isn’t free. She is the plastic cosmetic bag in an Ulta carousel. She is a throw pillow in a World Market bin. Her name and image might be the most commodified of the 20th century, so ubiquitous that she feels emptied of meaning. Or is she?

Relying primarily on the testimony of Mexican voices, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, a new documentary by Trisha Ziff, poses this question across a colorful spectrum of socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history. “I learned about Communism from Frida’s bookshelf,” shares actress and activist Ofelia Medina, who visited Kahlo’s home on a sixth-grade field trip.

“Frida gave me strength, she gave me a life and a job,” explains Juana López Sánchez, an Indigenous artisan whose livelihood is selling hand-crafted Frida dolls in Mexico City.

Latinx Artists Are the Fresh Visionaries

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization.
  • It has been revealed that over the past several years, I have documented the work of Latinx creatives across public art, fashion, and independent filmmaking, and I believe we have every reason to feel unabashedly optimistic.
  • According to recent reports, sometimes, their methods involve elevating vernacular and popular culture to expand traditional aesthetic repertoires.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry: Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.

It has been revealed that over the past several years, I have documented the work of Latinx creatives across public art, fashion, and independent filmmaking, and I believe we have every reason to feel unabashedly optimistic. Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins. They are using culture to reclaim heritage and reframe the narrative. This marks a distinct departure from older paradigms, where artists were taught — or forced — to believe that conforming to mainstream, assimilationist models was the only path to success. While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.

According to recent reports, sometimes, their methods involve elevating vernacular and popular culture to expand traditional aesthetic repertoires. We see this in contemporary fashion with designers like Willy Chavarria and Raul Lopez (Luar), who draw from working-class aesthetics, immigrant youth, and urban street culture. Most importantly, these designers openly credit their sources of inspiration, making clear that Mexican-American communities and neighborhoods and Black and Brown queer nightlife are fashion-forward in and of themselves. They frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways.

According to recent reports, in other cases, artists reassess their communities' histories to directly challenge historical marginalization, as seen in the work of Gina Gwen Palacios in Brownsville, Texas. As SpaceX expands across the region, treating the land as empty of people and culture and ripe for corporate speculation, Palacios centers the rich legacy of Mexican-American communities and their direct links to the present. Through paintings that highlight her family’s legacy as fieldworkers alongside the underrepresented landscape of South Texas, Palacios elevates everyday elements such as nopales and mesquite trees to tell stories of migration, hard labor, and policing.

Against the settler-colonial myths propagated by SpaceX pundits, artist-led projects in the area, such as Boca Chica, Corazón Grande, have focused on crowdsourcing archival materials from residents to uplift their deep roots in the region. This effort reaffirms Boca Chica Beach’s identity as "the people’s beach," directly challenging claims that Brownsville and Rio Grande Valley communities are devoid of people and value, and merely sites for space debuts, by centering residents' memories and their continued symbolic and living ties to the land.

The political significance of these types of projects cannot be overstated. While Guadalupe Rosales's landmark archival initiative Veteranas and Rucas has garnered considerable recognition in art circles, similar crowdsourced, post-custodial digital archives are emerging across Latinx communities nationwide. Examples include Nuevayorkinos, Documenting the Nameplate, Rhizomes: Mexican American Art Since 1848, and, of course, Boca Chica, Corazón Grande. By inviting community contributions, these platforms deliver the empowering message that everyone's history is inherently worthy of analysis and documentation.

Recent findings suggest that this spirit is also evident in Upcoming York City’s public art, where artists are Latinizing the cityscape through projects that draw on marginalized elements of history, such as Afro-Indigenous heritage and the city’s Latinx and multicultural history, challenging the erasure of their presence across the city’s memorial and monument landscape. Melissa Calderón, the first Latina to create a permanent public monument in the city, paid homage to Roberto Clemente with “Para Roberto” (2019), the first monument of its kind in the Bronx. Maria Magdalena Campos Pons’s “Procession of Angels for Radical Love and Unity” (2024) reframed New York City’s history from the perspective of its Black and brown residents in a performance filled with Orisha Santeria references. That same year, Edra Soto’s “Graft” (2024–25) took over the Doris C. Freedman Plaza in Central Park, inaugurating a sculptural installation drawing on Caribbean and Puerto Rican vernacular architecture. Think also of David Rios’s “Get Carried Away, You have the Right” (2023), drawing on Afro-Taino futuristic images in his installation at Amtrak, and Shellyne Rodriguez’s “Phoenix Ladder: Monument to the People of the Bronx” (2025), a reproduction of a Bronx building evoking the borough’s strength and rebuilding after the 1970s fires.

It is true that many of these artists remain marginalized, navigating a chronic lack of opportunities and resources. Consider the last time you saw a film by award-winning independent Latinx directors like Cecilia Aldarondo or Diana Peralta on a mainstream streaming home screen or in a theater. Yet when we look at the work itself — its courage, its artistry, and its local impact — the movement is undeniably transformative. It demonstrates that Latinx communities are resilient and that art and culture are powerful tools of empowerment and continuity.

It has been revealed that this realization is vital not just for us, but for society at large. Appreciating Latinx art offers a clear path beyond the polarized, distorted representations that have dominated public discourse for so long. The narratives Latinx artists uplift are the very ones everyone must champion as we navigate the rapid rise of AI technology and the growth of violent capitalism. Artists in the Rio Grande Valley, for example, are fiercely defending the intrinsic value of their environment and history, reminding us that community and culture are ultimately priceless. Others are also confronting traditional histories and value hierarchies within creative industries while redefining what is considered fashionable, memorable, and significant.

It has been revealed that most importantly, artists’ visions have the potential to generate change in all of us. This work actively transforms the lives of future generations: raised with powerful models of resistance against dehumanization and persecution, their imaginations will remain free.

Arlene Dávila's fresh book, Visualizing Latinx: Creative Practices in Fashion, Film, and Beyond (2026), is now out through Duke University Press.

#22277. What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind

What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work.
  • Recent findings suggest that the work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge.
  • According to recent reports, the result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work. Her oeuvre includes signature large blackened canvases, marked by fluid, ecstatic gestures in neon paint that resemble the glowing afterimages of a moving flame. O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, Requiem, is a fitting self-elegy for the painter precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.

Recent findings suggest that the work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge. O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them.

According to recent reports, the result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997). The black, fingerlike marks that protrude from the surrounding deep navy seem to be reaching for the floral clusters and reeds in the painting’s top half, like a perpetual grasping at splendor in the shadows.

In a recent development, though non-representational, these works continually approach figuration, filled with partial outlines of human and animal forms. These half-figures peer through their dark surroundings, like the pink mass in the center of “What’s Time to a Pig” (c. 1990s), and are caught in a constant state of emergence. Like an act of divine creation, O’Neal captures the transformation of raw material into something seemingly miraculous through the hands of a master craftsman.

During this formative and fruitful period between the 1970s and 1990s, when her visual language and iconoclastic artistic sensibility crystallized, O’Neal was also coming into her own as an artist. She was a groundbreaking student, becoming the first Black woman to receive an MFA from Columbia University in 1969, and in 1985, she became the first African American professor to receive tenure in UC Berkeley’s Department of Art Practice.

Industry observers note that the back room offers a rich sketch of the painter’s life as it intersected with both world history and art history. Born in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1942, Jim Crow was fully in place in the American South during the artist’s childhood. She attended Howard University in 1960 alongside David Driskell and Lois Mailou Jones, dated the activist Stokely Carmichael, and was an activist in her own right.

According to recent reports, the archival materials reveal the cultural and political concerns of O’Neal’s time. It’s all the more remarkable that she navigated these constraints while retaining the verve and genuine, delightful strangeness these paintings must have necessitated. “Untitled” (n.d.) gets at the humor and irreverence of O’Neal’s style. An Uncle Sam-like figure, half-covered in chalky white paint, evokes a satirical Ralph Bakshi cartoon, with many identifying features erased. It has a winking quality. Though political in nature, it foregrounds O’Neal’s formal concerns, which circle mainly around the possibilities of certain pigments (like the enveloping darkness of lampblack contrasted with punchy neons) and the permeable boundary between abstraction and figuration. It is this formal rigor that made O’Neal trailblazing in more ways than one –– both as a Black American shattering institutional barriers and as a woman painter making key interventions into the inherited, lionized artistic movements of the Color Field, Abstract Expressionism, and Minimalism.

Mary Lovelace O'Neal, "Race Woman Series #7" (1992-93), mixed media on canvas (left); Mary Lovelace O'Neal, "Untitled" (n.d.), mixed media and oil on canvas.

“Race Woman Series #7” (1992–93) dramatizes the tension between the structural or compositional and the political, suggesting that it was an enduring preoccupation for the artist. A dazed face vaguely springs up from a prominent green being, which could just be read as an indecipherable scrawl, while a white specter at the top of the canvas drips over it. O’Neal’s use of color is frenetic and instinctive, resulting in a painting that is too varied to slot into a clear interpretation. Like the Klannish chiaroscuro of Norman Lewis’ “Alabama” (1960), the legibility of “Race Woman Series #7” relies on the light its instructive title sheds on it.

But unlike Lewis, when we search for correlation between O’Neal’s caption and the canvas, we are pulled deeper into her self-reflexive, numinous and unrepeatable idiom, which makes its own intuitive sense and, anyway, seeks to go beyond sense-making into the terrain of near-mystical experience.

Mary Lovelace O’Neal: Requiem continues at Boesky Gallery (509 West 24th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan) through December 19. The exhibition is organized by the gallery.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it reveals across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.

Industry observers note that the culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?).

Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015, among other instances of artwashing. They penned a joint review of Italian curator and organizer Marco Baravalle’s book The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism, a toolkit for seeing through the mainstream art world’s undermining of political movements and building sustainable alternatives.

Critic Carolina A. Miranda, meanwhile, takes up two fresh books by East Los Angeles artist Guadalupe Rosales, who came up in a community of Chicano kids raised in the 1990s amid uprisings and political action. Miranda writes that the anthology Rosales edited, as well as her blended memoir and photo book, perfectly encapsulate “the ways she engages the stories of others even as she tells her own.” A wise observation to carry with us as we face the week ahead; more of the latest in art book reviews and news below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht has used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

Licht Kunst Licht (LKL) collaborated with RheinEnergie and the Dombauhütte Köln restoration workshop to develop a lighting concept for Cologne‘s historic cathedral, which is also Germany’s most visited landmark.

Prior to the intervention, it was primarily illuminated using floodlights placed atop nearby buildings. These 1,000-watt metal halide lamps consumed a great deal of energy and, according to LKL, flooded the building in an unflattering neutral white light.

LKL replaced this broad-brush approach with discreet, warm-spectrum LED fixtures, illuminating the building’s Gothic features by providing subtle backlighting combined with vertical grazing light to enliven the ornate facades.

“The central concept ‘light follows architecture’ replaces indiscriminate floodlighting with targeted illumination,” the studio explained.

“Instead of flattening the facade, light is directed to articulate depth, rhythm and verticality. The outcome is a sculptural night presence while the luminaires remain largely invisible by day.”.

In a recent development, the project’s key innovation was the development of bespoke, multifunctional lighting poles that are covertly integrated into the structure using custom clamps to protect the stonework. The aim was to render the fixtures “largely invisible” during the day and allow them to be dismantled without impacting the historic structure.

Each pole contains a glare-free light module used to provide facade or circulation lighting that is fully dimmable and can be adapted to events, seasons and ecological needs.

According to lighting designer and LKL project lead Philipp Schmitz, a lack of detailed architectural plans necessitated an extensive study of the facades to ensure the intricate Gothic details were suitably illuminated.

“Because digital simulations were insufficient for such a complex, heterogeneous structure, we conducted years of extensive on-site lighting tests, experimenting with optics, angles and positions to achieve the desired effects through empirical observation,” he pointed out.

It has been revealed that only 10 per cent of the light now comes from fixtures located away from the building, compared to 80 per cent previously. This reduces unwanted light scatter and improves precision, while long-wave light reduces disruption to nocturnal species.

A series of minimalist stainless-steel lighting pylons on the cathedral plaza now illuminate entrances and highlight selected facade elements.

Sustainability was a key consideration throughout the project, with overall energy consumption reduced by 80 per cent while delivering improved visual quality, according to LKL.

Cologne Cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Cologne and is a renowned monument of German Catholicism and Gothic architecture.

Industry observers note that construction began in 1248 but was halted around 1560 and then restarted in the 19th century, with the building finally completed to its original medieval initiative in 1880. The cathedral, which was briefly the world’s tallest building upon its completion, went on to be declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.

Dezeen readers crowned LKL’s scheme lighting design of the year in the public vote at this year’s Dezeen Awards. The project is now in the running to be crowned overall winner by a jury of leading industry figures including Norman Foster, Michael Anastassiades and Jaime Hayon.

Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (454 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hyperallergic

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that looking to cash in on marquee week in Newly introduced York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17.
  • The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy.
  • A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that looking to cash in on marquee week in Newly introduced York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million.

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy. In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections.

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic strategy, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”.

It has been revealed that the de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.

Sources indicate that “Yellow River” emerged from a series of “highway" paintings representing the artist's shift from cacophonous urban compositions to more airy landscapes, designating the freeway as a conduit connecting New York City to the Hudson River Valley and Long Island's South Fork. In vibrant warm yellow, earthy brown tones, and stretches of deep blue, de Kooning's decisive gestures direct viewers across overlapping paths and visual rest stops throughout the canvas.

In a recent development, “I love to be on those highways,” de Kooning said to British critic and curator David Sylvester about the expansive roads during a BBC interview in 1960. “And they are really not very pretty, but the big embankments and the shoulders of the roads and the curves are flawless.”.

“Yellow River” hung at the foot of Solinger's bed for some time, serving as a testament to Solinger's fascination with the artist. His wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, took ownership of the work after Solinger passed in 1996, and in 2011, she designated the work as a promised gift to the Whitney in honor of her late husband. It officially entered the Whitney's holdings in 2023, the same year that the museum deaccessioned seven works, including an Edward Hopper landscape, and sent them to auction to benefit the collection.

  • “By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government has temporarily blocked two 16th-century volumes of Mughal calligraphy from being taken out of the country permanently.

The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

“By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved. Given so few works of this kind survive intact, its preservation makes it especially valuable,” states a statement from the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The volumes were kept in a private collection from the 1980s until 2020 when they were sold at Sotheby’s London for £620,000 (before fees) to a specialist dealer in London.

In a recent development, the calligraphic works, thought to be over 400 years old, are spread across 29 leaves and feature gold ornamentation of plant and animal motifs. The two volumes derive from an imperial album created around 1595-1605.

In a recent development, according to the DCMS statement, the original album was prepared for Mughal Emperor Akbar or his son Prince Salim at the royal workshop either in Lahore or Agra. Muhammad Hussain Kashmiri and Abd al-Rahim al-Haravi are among the calligraphers featured.

The Black Prince marble bust by Michael Rysbrack (around 1735).

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.

In a recent development, meanwhile another export bar has been placed on a marble bust of the 14th-century prince Edward of Woodstock, the son of King Edward III of England and popularly known as the Black Prince. Created around 1735, the sculpture was made by the Flemish sculptor, Michael Rysbrack.

This export bar will initially expire on 5 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £496,044 plus VAT, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Fiona Twycross, the heritage minister, indicates in a statement: “For nearly three hundred years [the sculpture] has shaped how we tell the story of our medieval history and I hope that in a public gallery in the UK it can tell that story much more powerfully for many more years to come.”.

#22269. Access to Shanghai Grand Opera House staircase restricted to paid ticket holders

Access to Shanghai Grand Opera House staircase restricted to paid ticket holders

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Kaia Wang, Yumeng Zhu, Tian Fangfang, Chen Hao.
  • The Snøhetta-designed Shanghai Grand Opera House has introduced a paid ticketing system for visitors wanting to access the signature spiral staircase and rooftop viewing platform at the recently opened building in Shanghai.
  • It has been revealed that when Dezeen visited the site, we observed a temporary barricade separating the free-to-access ground-level public space from the spiral staircase leading up to the roof.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Kaia Wang, Yumeng Zhu, Tian Fangfang, Chen Hao.

The Snøhetta-designed Shanghai Grand Opera House has introduced a paid ticketing system for visitors wanting to access the signature spiral staircase and rooftop viewing platform at the recently opened building in Shanghai.

It has been revealed that when Dezeen visited the site, we observed a temporary barricade separating the free-to-access ground-level public space from the spiral staircase leading up to the roof. Access to the staircase and roof now costs 50 yuan (£5.60) per person.

Since opening, access to the architectural feature has been restricted, with visitors now required to pre-book tickets online to access it between 10:30 am and 2:30 pm. According to the booking site, people with tickets to see a performance inside the opera house are still required to purchase a ticket, and the fee includes accident insurance.

Asked about the apparent change in access requirements, Snøhetta said that demand meant that “visitor management is necessary” and that “access arrangements will continue to develop”.

“As with any major cultural institution, operational procedures continue to evolve during the opening period as the Opera House team gains experience with visitor patterns, capacity needs, and the building’s day-to-day use,” the studio told Dezeen.

“Given the exceptional public interest and the limited capacity of the roof and public stairs, visitor management is necessary to ensure a safe and enjoyable experience for everyone,” it continued.

“Access arrangements will continue to develop with operational experience, but the intention remains the same: to create a building that can be widely enjoyed by the public while balancing accessibility, safety, and the visitor experience.”.

Following news that a fee had been introduced, the phrase “is it worth spending 50 yuan to visit Shanghai Grand Opera House” trended on Chinese social media.

Some commenters questioned whether charging to visit the attraction was justifiable, while others sympathised with the need for crowd control. Others shared tips on how to take the best photos of the building without paying the entrance fee.

Visitors Dezeen spoke to at the site were concerned about both the fee and the temporary barriers.

In a recent development, “I don’t think it’s worth the money,” Mr Qiu, who paid to climb the stairs, told Dezeen. “Basically you pay to climb a giant stair. If you want good photos of the stairs, best to take from afar, which you can do for free,”.

Ms Ye, who didn’t pay the entry fee, told Dezeen that she was really disappointed that the barricade was in her photos.

Industry observers note that “I don’t know what the point of the barricade is – to separate the paid and unpaid? Or for better crowd circulation? But at least they need to put some effort into designing it to match the beauty of the building,” she noted.

“It really is an eyesore for the photos.”.

According to recent reports, the building, and its accessible roof, are often compared to Oslo Opera House, which was also designed by Snøhetta and is topped with a walkable roof. According to the studio, both projects were designed to “reduce thresholds wherever possible”.

“Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors, and ticketed programs,” said Snøhetta co-founder Kjetil Thorsen at the time of the Shanghai Grand Opera House opening.

“We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue. People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city,” he continued.

“A successful landmark is not only recognised by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives.”.

According to recent reports, several other cultural projects in China have been built with publicly accessible roofs. However, the accessibility presented in concepts has often been restricted when the buildings open.

It has been revealed that also in Shanghai, the Start Museum, designed by French architect Jean Nouvel and opened in 2022, features a public roof that can be used for displaying large-scale artwork. However, the space has rarely been used.

The Amateur Architecture Studio-designed Fuchun Cultural Museum Complex is defined by a continuous undulating roof to resemble the experience of climbing the local Fuchun Mountain. However, the roof didn’t open to the public for four years and is now only open to public visits for one hour a day, three days a week.

Kaia Wang contributed to the story.

#22268. Why Dispatch's creators said no to '10,000 endings'

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1207 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq ↗ Open Full Page

Why Dispatch's creators said no to '10,000 endings'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every interactive story faces the same temptation: give the player more.
  • Recent findings suggest that as the breakout indie game celebrates its one-year anniversary with the Dispatch Deluxe Edition, which lets you play the storyboard art, I caught up with the team.
  • According to recent reports, adHoc starts with the belief that most developers get the equation backwards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every interactive story faces the same temptation: give the player more. More branches, more endings, more ways to bend the script until it snaps. Dispatch, AdHoc Studio's episodic superhero workplace comedy, went the other way. It stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, who now sends a team of reformed villains out on call-outs.

Recent findings suggest that as the breakout indie game celebrates its one-year anniversary with the Dispatch Deluxe Edition, which lets you play the storyboard art, I caught up with the team. We've heard how Four video tracks and a doughnut shop got it started and how AdHoc made Dispatch feel like an animated TV series, so now I want to know how a choice-driven game gets that far by holding choices back. We put the question to AdHoc co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors.

According to recent reports, adHoc starts with the belief that most developers get the equation backwards. "When folks set out to make an interactive narrative game, they incorrectly assume that it's all about the branching narrative that makes it exciting," Herman says. "We believe it's about the quality of that narrative at the core, and then you have to branch that quality narrative.".

That's easy to say and hard to do, he admits, and harder still when you have to write multiple good stories at once, which is what the team signed up for. So the development team works from the story's spine and its characters, then figure out what choice space could believably exist alongside them.

Industry observers note that robert Robertson arrives with a backstory and a personality, so options that betray him are off the table. Herman sees that as a gift: it "eliminates blue sky" and lets the team concentrate on a believable character. It's also why he's wary when people ask for thousands of endings. Would 10,000 of them really be as compelling as a six or seven that the team has made as satisfying as possible?

Lenart describes the whole process as "almost an exercise in restraint at times". Picture 10 developers in a room discussing a scene where a character is aggressive towards you. A couple of them will say they wish you could just punch him. "The thing we have to filter that through is, 'Would Robert conceivably punch him in this situation?'" claims Lenart. "A lot of times the answer is no.".

It isn't a flat ban. If everyone agrees that punching him would be thrilling but there's no motivation for it, Herman notes the conversation becomes how to make it a viable choice. Lenart says you go back into the scene and the story and set it up "so that that choice feels like it's a payoff to something that exists".

Skip that groundwork and the cost is steep. "The more you do that, the more you start diluting your character and then they kind of become a little bit faceless," Lenart warns. Herman puts it more bluntly: the story starts to feel like "a narrative toy" and less like one with believable characters.

Sources indicate that so how do you make a choice feel weighty without animating an entirely new story? Lenart states, "A lot of the magic in these types of games is the story that people are telling in their heads". The most effective choices, he says, are the ones where "you're affecting how another character in the story thinks about you".

It has been revealed that treat someone a certain way in front of the group, and players will assume that character's later behaviour is motivated by it. Every glance in a later scene gets read as payback for what you remarked earlier, which Lenart compares to real life. AdHoc builds on that expectation on purpose.

Recent findings suggest that herman calls it "the grease between the major cogs of choices". Players carry a decision forward for an hour or so, until the grease runs out and they need an injection of newly introduced stuff. If a scene doesn't land that way, he notes, "it's probably because something's broken". Contrivance, or a sense of being guided, are the signs to go back and fix.

There's a hard budget reason for the discipline too. "It's also just so expensive to do it the way we're doing it," says Herman, with a vision for cinematic quality and animation that makes 30 different endings impossible.

Lenart gives an example of a branch the team could have offered. Imagine letting players choose at the start whether Robert works as a dispatcher or makes a new suit and heads off to be a hero in another city. It sounds great on a flowchart, but "you'd end up animating an entirely different game", with two separate stories, and Robert's arc would stop being about redemption.

Herman is generous about other approaches. He points to Slay the Princess, The Stanley Parable, and Detroit: Become Human as games where their branchiness and reactivity are major selling points. "Interactive narrative games are not one thing," he indicates. "The beauty of the medium is that everyone finds ways to express it in different ways.".

Where does the line fall between what the player controls and what stays with the writers and developers? Lenart says it comes down to how much agency AdHoc is willing to hand over in order to tell a story it believes in. The more it gives up, the greater the risk of versions that aren't great. "Our goal was always to make it so that any path you play through is compelling and satisfying.".

Sources indicate that there's a cost, and AdHoc accepts it. Herman says some players will end up on a path that isn't their preference, and with stories it gets personal: "this isn't how I wanted it to go.".

Lenart has seen the other side of the argument. On earlier games, multiple endings were mandated as a studio priority, and the takeaway was that "some of them worked". Some people had good playthroughs, others got endings they weren't satisfied with, and some were upset they didn't get the endings their friends did.

Sources indicate that he doesn't count loose ends as a failure, either. "Not every story or movie you watch ends with you thinking everything is perfect and wrapped up," he says, and the threads people talk about afterwards are part of the experience. But "it can get out of hand if you don't keep it under control".

Industry News: How Playstation nailed its iconic startup screen

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a short ritual that plays out every time someone switches on a PlayStation.
  • For more than thirty years, every generation of PlayStation has opened with its own version of this sequence.
  • Industry observers note that that intent goes back to the beginning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a short ritual that plays out every time someone switches on a PlayStation. You press the power button and, before the dashboard appears, movement and sound take over, building through a sequence before the console hands you over to play. It lasts only seconds, but those seconds have a beginning, a build, a pause and a release. They are designed as an experience in their own right.

For more than thirty years, every generation of PlayStation has opened with its own version of this sequence. The motion, visual language and sound have changed but the decision to design that transition has remained. What could easily be functional downtime has instead become part of the PlayStation experience. It rivals the best motion in logo design, but it also has its own function as well.

Industry observers note that that intent goes back to the beginning. When Manabu Sakamoto designed the original PlayStation logo, he wanted it to capture one of the console’s defining promises: 3D. The interlocking P and S created a sense of depth and space rather than simply sitting flat on a 2D screen. By spring 1994, that identity had been turned into an animation, handed to sound designer Takafumi Fujisawa as what the team called a “motion logo.”.

Recent findings suggest that fujisawa was given little direction beyond that animation and had to set the tone himself, working within tight technical limits. He wanted the startup to feel like walking into a cinema. That particular hush where you sense something is about to begin.

Sources indicate that A straight cut from power-on to interface would give you a change of state and nothing else. Motion gives those few seconds structure; sound and visual design give them character. They are all working together, but motion is what determines how the experience unfolds through time.

It has been revealed that the startup’s primary job isn’t just to create an ‘atmosphere’, as it also helps organise the experience of entering the console itself. The sequence tells the player that something is happening, creates a sense of progression, and makes the eventual handoff into play feel deliberate.

On the original PlayStation, it took on a more practical role. The startup sound helped confirm that the hardware was running correctly and that the disc had been read. If it hadn’t, part of the sound was designed to loop to signal that something was wrong.

The important point is that the startup was not simply decoration sitting on top of a technical process. Motion, sound and visual design were part of how that process was communicated and felt.

That is where motion becomes especially useful. It can signal change, control pace, create anticipation and prepare someone for what comes next.

According to recent reports, over time, the original function of that startup changed. Hardware changed, interfaces changed, and the need to tell a player that a disc had been successfully read stopped mattering. Yet, PlayStation kept designing the transition.

Five generations on, those startups have looked, moved and sounded very different. What has survived through that time is the expectation that switching on any PlayStation from PS1 to PS5 deserves an authored beginning.

That consistency does not always come from repeating the same expression. It sometimes (and in this case) comes from recognising which moments are the most valuable. PlayStation could change the way those seconds looked and felt because the thing it had established beforehand went beyond the mere execution of it.

According to recent reports, brands spend enormous amounts of time designing the things people see, whether it be the best logos, typefaces, colours, layouts or interfaces. But experiences are also full of moments between those things.

Industry observers note that when an app opens, or a payment completes, an audience waits for something to begin. These transitions are easy to treat as functional gaps, especially when the instinct is to get people to the next thing as quickly as possible. The point, though, is not to add friction; it is to recognise that these moments already exist, and that repeated transitions can become part of the brand experience when they are deliberately designed.

Motion matters disproportionately in those spaces because it works in the same material the moment is made of: time. It determines how one state becomes another, and how that change is experienced along the way. PlayStation was able to make that transition worth designing and returning to in its own right.

Andrew Vucko merges a lifelong interest in motion and design with a passion for brand building. As the founder of Vucko, he leads a global motion studio that transforms brands like Google, Meta, and Spotify through award-winning motion identities, systems, and guidelines.

In a recent development, A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

The critical distinction is probate. In states with expensive or slow probate processes — California, New York, Florida, and many others — a living trust pays for itself many times over. In states with simplified probate procedures (like Texas or Wisconsin for small estates), the cost advantage of a trust is smaller but the privacy and incapacity benefits still apply.

Industry observers note that you need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

Recent findings suggest that the term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

It has been revealed that an irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:.

FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

Sources indicate that for most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

It has been revealed that nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, Upcoming Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate proposal.

Sources indicate that the remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

Recent findings suggest that the most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate initiative.

Recent findings suggest that A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific problems or complex situations.

It has been revealed that yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

Sources indicate that A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

The living trust vs will decision is not about which is better — it is about which is better for your specific situation. For estates with more than $100,000 in probatable assets, especially in high-cost probate states, a revocable living trust saves thousands of dollars and months of delay while providing incapacity protection and privacy that a will cannot match. For smaller estates in simplified-probate states, a well-drafted will with proper beneficiary designations may be all you need. Either way, the worst estate plan is no estate plan. More than 60% of American adults have neither a will nor a trust, leaving their families to navigate probate without guidance, pay avoidable costs, and endure unnecessary delays during the most difficult time of their lives.

Minimal merges small van and electric bike in Pedal 4 delivery vehicle

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Shortlisted in the consumer product design category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, Pedal 4 was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets.
  • The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle has a footprint not much larger than a bike – three metres by one metre – and is able to go down pedestrianised roads and use cycle infrastructure, according to Minimal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Minimal.

British start-up Minimal has designed an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van in the Pedal 4, now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

Shortlisted in the consumer product design category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, Pedal 4 was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets.

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle has a footprint not much larger than a bike – three metres by one metre – and is able to go down pedestrianised roads and use cycle infrastructure, according to Minimal.

At the same time, it boasts 2.5 cubic metres of cargo space and in London trials made 36 per cent more deliveries per hour than vans.

“Electric vans solve the emissions problem, but not the access problem,” said Minimal CEO and co-founder Patrick Bion. “They still sit in the same traffic, fight for the same kerb space and need a driver with a licence.”.

“They weren’t built for the job they’re doing,” he added. “We designed Pedal 4 around that job: a full round of deliveries, through streets a van can’t get down, ridden by anyone who can ride a bike.”.

Minimal considers the Pedal 4 to be not just an electrified van or scaled-up bicycle, but a vehicle engineered specifically for delivery with an aesthetic drawn directly from its functional architecture.

It has a four-wheeled base for stability and independent double-wishbone suspension at the front and a rubber torsion axle suspension system at the rear to help keep it level around corners, even when its cargo box is full.

The team removed the traditional bike chain, minimised fasteners and reduced part counts with the aim of making the vehicle both rugged enough for its task and easily serviceable.

They wanted the vehicle’s aesthetic to come directly from its functional architecture – an exposed zinc-coated carbon steel frame with satin black metal covers.

“Pedal 4 has to do a van’s job every day for years, so it can’t be fragile, fussy or expensive,” mentioned Minimal product design engineer Sean Heany. “Our biggest wins came from deleting parts, not adding features.”.

“By rethinking the geometry, we cut part count and fastenings, which made the vehicle tougher, quicker to fix and cheaper to build in our London microfactory.”.

The Pedal 4 includes two slots for swappable batteries, which lift out to charge outside of the vehicle and together give a range of 60 kilometres.

In the UK, the vehicle is classed as a heavy-duty electrically power-assisted cycle (EPAC) and can be driven without a licence, which Minimal notes widens the pool of people who can do the job.

It has been revealed that however, Minimal believes that the future of logistics lies in autonomous and worker-driven vehicles working side by side. To that end, each Pedal 4 is equipped with the company’s FleetOS fleet management software, which tracks its route and vehicle performance.

According to recent reports, minimal says that the data collected will be used to make the next round of design changes and inform the tech giant’s autonomous vehicle programme. Recently, it has launched Bot, a UK- and EU-focused delivery robot.

Recent findings suggest that “Pedal 4 is where our autonomy work starts,” mentioned Heaney. “Every vehicle is connected, and more than 100,000 kilometres of real delivery data has taught us what city logistics actually demands.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The same principles carry over: fewer parts, lower cost, built for uptime. They are what make autonomy work economically, not just technically.”.

Sources indicate that pedal 4 has been engineered for, tested on and now released on London’s streets through partners Royal Mail and Evri, but Heaney claims the same vehicles and software are built to scale across Europe. The tech giant prepares to launch in the US in 2027.

“London is one of the hardest places in the world to deliver, which makes it the best place to start,” said Heaney. “If Pedal 4 works on London’s streets, it can work anywhere.”.

Industry observers note that “Cities can’t keep moving goods the way they did last century,” he continued. “We need new ways of moving things that make our cities, our environment and our everyday lives better.”.

Other recent new electric vehicle typologies include the Amble One – a doorless electric buggy in the vein of a golf cart – and a three-wheeler called Trinity designed for urban travel.

Photography courtesy of Minimal.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As creative software races toward increased automation, are we as designers asking the right questions?
  • Over the years, I’ve watched the conversations of web developers and designers shift increasingly toward technology, and further away from something we once took great pride in: Craft.
