📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As creative software races toward increased automation, are we as designers asking the right questions?

Over the years, I’ve watched the conversations of web developers and designers shift increasingly toward technology, and further away from something we once took great pride in: Craft.

Recent findings suggest that the 20th century was an extraordinary period for graphic design, particularly typography and print. By the 1990s we had inherited an astonishingly mature digital toolbox: QuarkXPress, Photoshop, PostScript typography and all the precision that came with them.

Those tools were deeply rooted in the crafts they replaced. Photoshop borrowed directly from the photographic darkroom – dodge, burn and all. Quark brought centuries of typographic practice into the digital workspace, giving designers extraordinarily precise control over type and composition.

Then we moved communications to the web – and somehow left much of that toolbox behind. Our web platforms never came close to giving designers the same depth of control. Many creatives simply accepted the loss and stated, “Well, that’s just the web.”.

I never quite bought into that. Instead I started making notes for what would become Design Studio for Gutenberg (DSG), a powerful designer-first plugin for WordPress Gutenberg.

And at this moment, an inflection point when creative software makers increasingly want to automate design itself, we need to ask: Could better tools offer another way forward?

Web typography has always been a particular sore point for me.

Industry observers note that I’ll admit my standards may be unusually high. I cut my typography chops as a Type Director at J. Walter Type, part of the legendary JWT ad agency, and such training is hard to shake.

According to recent reports, so I found workarounds for maintaining the quality my clients expected. For example, for notable headlines I would often set the type in Illustrator, kern it properly, export it as SVG artwork and bring that into a website as art.

Ridiculous? Perhaps. But my clients included brands like American Express, Merck and Lincoln Center. They expected high-quality work, and I delivered. But there had to be a better way.

As each newly introduced web-design platform arrived, I would look to see whether somebody had finally built one from a designer’s point of view. A typographer's point of view. Many claimed they had. But mostly they just gave us what programmers thought designers wanted.

Recent findings suggest that eventually I stopped waiting. A few years ago I sat down with my studio’s programmers and gave them a simple directive:We are going to build what designers need.

WordPress was the obvious foundation. It was open source, mature and unlikely to disappear like so many web-dev programs before it.

Sources indicate that my other directive: Design Studio could not be another heavy page-builder sitting on top of WordPress. It needed to live inside Gutenberg and thus benefit from WordPress’ lighter weight and faster core.

We even created our own mantra: WordPress Builds Webpages. DSG Designs Them.

According to recent reports, we methodically broke down what was missing. The list grew fast.

We ultimately ended up creating a system with THREE BLOCKS, one custom TEMPLATE, and more UI additions and tools than I could count.

Let’s start with the three blocks, which contain tools you simply will not find in other web-development systems:.

Recent findings suggest that this text block is unique. It has every major type control that you might have found in Quark or InDesign. Powerful tools like KERNING, without which we can never hope to produce professional grade typography.

It has been revealed that font choices in TDB are not tied to any template. Instead they allow full font and style selections just like a desktop app. And it works directly with our font management system found in the DESIGNER DASH backend (more on that later).

It also allows mixed type, font, style and more, all within a single text container.

A friend testing DSG at a major ad agency said it best: “Composite layers in WP? Mind blown.”.

Sources indicate that import multilayer Photoshop or Krita files (see my comparison of those two here), then treat each layer independently with blur, invert, halftone, sepia and full BLEND settings. Then each layer can be easily scaled, rotated, and even placed anywhere on the page.

In a recent development, this tool is simply fun. Go play with it in our LIVE DEMO.

This full-width block offers real freedom. Starting with a HEIGHT CONTROL slider, so no more needing to wedge in spacers or scaffolding.

Within the Composition Block, TDB and ADB can be placed freely anywhere you want. Even overlapping each other, or hanging off the CB. (Our website is the perfect example.).

Some early testers had to look twice to make sure they were still in WordPress.

Industry observers note that we knew just what they meant: Rulers, Guides, Grid, device-specific Visibility icons across every object in the List View. We include a very special BLANK CANVAS template, better page controls, and a backend DESIGNER DASH with tabs for Font.

According to recent reports, my goal here isn’t to catalog every Design Studio for Gutenberg feature. I mention these to make a larger point: Web designers deserve better tools. And that feels particularly vital now.

AI has an enormous role to play in our future creative work. Let it remove drudgery, generate first passes, organise assets and automate anything that doesn’t benefit from human judgment.

But craft begins where the default answer ends. “Craft” has always been, and shall always remain a very human thing.

Recent findings suggest that craft is deciding that two letters need to be kerned tighter. That an image needs to move three pixels down. That this composition should deliberately break the grid. That the mobile version shouldn’t simply be a smaller copy of the desktop.

According to recent reports, those are precisely the kinds of decisions that only professional designers should make. And it requires precision tools like those in DSG that allow such decisions to be executed.

After reading the DSG manual, I asked ChatGPT how its own web-building abilities compared with those of a competent designer using DSG. Its answer was spot-on:.

“A surprising amount of what DSG enables is still awkward to get from AI.” — ChatGPT.

It has been revealed that in my mind it is not a question of human vs. AI. But instead, how to use the best tools for each part of your job.

Sources indicate that we built a live demo so you can come kick the tires. And because we are very substantial on sharing in general, and the open source, free and affordable software movements, we are releasing Design Studio for Gutenberg, with everything we have talked about and so much more for just $39. Including per-person unlimited use (right, that means no more counting websites), and a license that never expires.

In a recent development, with the release of Design Studio 1.0 we hope to contribute to the goal of building a better web. This is step one.

Visit Design Studio for Gutenberg, try the DEMO: https://openstudiony.com.

Lance Evans is creative director of Graphlink Media (graphlink.com), a boutique creative marketing agency in NYC, with clients like Olive Garden, Miller Beer and AMEX. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

It has been revealed that the act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Recent findings suggest that whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

It has been revealed that psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

Industry observers note that one 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

Recent findings suggest that however, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Sources indicate that tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It states, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

📅 03 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.
  • Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal.
  • European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins states about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal concerns and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Recent findings suggest that two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins indicates about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

In a recent development, “She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins claims this concept can lend to beauty standards.

It has been revealed that when it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins claims you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins states change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

  • American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny that was informed by conversations with Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza.
  • Named The Sculpture Watch, the timepiece has a dial that includes four intersecting blocks of colour within a circular case that resembles a watch designed by Siza for Cauny.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Nuno Sousa Dias unless stated.

American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny that was informed by conversations with Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza.

Named The Sculpture Watch, the timepiece has a dial that includes four intersecting blocks of colour within a circular case that resembles a watch designed by Siza for Cauny.

According to Holl, his watch was designed to be a dialogue between the two architects and was directly informed by a compliment the Portuguese architect once gave him.

Recent findings suggest that “On July 25, 2018, I gave a summer lecture in at the Porto Academy,” Holl told Dezeen. “Siza came to my talk and came up to me after and said ‘Steven, you use colour like Matisse, I must try in my next project’.”.

“Siza is the greatest living architect,” he continued. “I will never forget that afternoon. This watch is an homage to Alvaro Siza,”.

The Sculpture Watch has a three-dimensional dial with the red, green, yellow and blue colour blocks raised on top of each other.

Industry observers note that it was intended as a direct translation of Holl’s watercolour paintings that were complimented by Siza. Holl is well known for his painting and begins the majority of his architecture projects with a small watercolour sketch.

“Watercolor painting, integral to my design process for architecture, inspires this timepiece,” noted Holl.

“The colour volumes on the dial are made of brass; well-tested in watchmaking and best to allow Cauny to reproduce the watercolours.”.

“My approach to colour is conceptual,” he continued.

It has been revealed that “I try to engage colour in the idea driving the design, like the ‘projected colour’ from unseen surfaces in the DE Shaw trading floor, or the complimentary colours in the ‘seven bottles of light’ in our Chapel of St. Ignatius, which is analogous to the Jesuit spiritual exercises.”.

Holl also reflected on how colour can reflect the passing of time.

“Time is marked in a personal way, with each moment its own polychrome experience,” he noted.

According to recent reports, “Colour turns time’s passage into both a visual and temporal experience. The fragility and variation of colour remind us that time is a human experience of duration.”.

The Sculpture Watch is the fifth piece created for Cauny in its The Architects of Time Series. Following Siza, who designed the first timepiece in the collection, architects Rafael Moneo, Eduardo Souto Moura and Tadao Ando have designed watches for the brand.

Numerous high-profile architects have turned their hands to watch design and we recently rounded up six watches designed by Pritzker Architecture Prize-winning architects.

Photography by Nuno Sousa Dias unless stated.

Arta Moves Beyond Shipping Art, to Helping Collectors Pay for It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, Arta has helped collectors get art from a gallery or an auction house to their homes.
  • The New York–based technology manufacturer has introduced Arta Pay, a new financing service that allows collectors to buy art, watches, jewelry, and other luxury goods on credit, paying for them over 10 months while sellers receive the full purchase price within days.
  • According to recent reports, the service offers credit lines ranging from $1,000 to more than $100,000, targeting a part of the market that has often fallen between conventional consumer financing and the large art loans offered by private banks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, Arta has helped collectors get art from a gallery or an auction house to their homes. Now, it wants to help them pay for it, too.

The New York–based technology manufacturer has introduced Arta Pay, a new financing service that allows collectors to buy art, watches, jewelry, and other luxury goods on credit, paying for them over 10 months while sellers receive the full purchase price within days.

According to recent reports, the service offers credit lines ranging from $1,000 to more than $100,000, targeting a part of the market that has often fallen between conventional consumer financing and the large art loans offered by private banks. Related Articles Sotheby's Dinosaur 'Jodi' Sells for $47.3 M., More Than Five Times Its High Estimate Monet Painting Sells for $56.2 M., Setting French Auction Record at Sotheby's Paris.

In a recent development, here’s how it works: A collector buying a $10,000 painting would put down at least 10 percent, or $1,000, and pay the remaining balance in nine monthly installments. There’s a flat financing charge of 12.5 percent on the amount borrowed, disclosed upfront. In this example, that would add $1,125 to the cost of the painting if the buyer takes the full nine months to repay it.

Recent findings suggest that the gallery, meanwhile, gets its $10,000 within five business days, without having to worry about collecting the remaining payments. Arta takes on the repayment and fraud risk, and charges sellers no processing fees.

It has been revealed that “We’ve spent years building the post-purchase technology that powers commerce across art, luxury, and collectibles,” Adam Fields, Arta’s founder and CEO, stated. The newly introduced service, he added, is designed to make the transactions easier.

In a recent development, arta has become a familiar name behind the scenes of the art market, providing shipping, insurance, and other logistical services to auction houses, galleries, and online marketplaces. Its clients include Sotheby’s, Bonhams, and Artsy, and the organization claims it has facilitated the movement of more than $1 billion worth of objects across more than 65 countries.

The move into financing brings Arta into an earlier stage of the transaction, when a collector is deciding whether to buy something in the first place.

Industry observers note that for galleries, the attraction is fairly straightforward. Many already allow trusted clients to pay in installments, but doing so can mean waiting months to receive the full price of a work. Arta Pay gives them a way to offer similar flexibility without extending credit themselves.

Industry observers note that the service can be used at online checkouts, in person, or through an ordinary invoice, a useful feature in a business where plenty of sales are still negotiated over email, WhatsApp, or a conversation at an art fair. Collectors can also apply for a credit line before deciding what to buy, using it across purchases from different sellers.

Among the first businesses to adopt the service are Rago Wright, the auction house group, and Swiss Watch Expo.

Industry observers note that “Our collectors want flexibility in how they buy, and Arta Pay gives them that,” Richard Wright, CEO of Rago Wright, noted in a statement. For the auction house, he added, the advantage is offering payment plans without having to manage the financing or assume the risk.

The idea isn’t entirely upcoming. Art Money, another firm that allowed collectors to buy art in installments, stopped taking new business in June 2024 after running out of operating capital. Its founder, Paul Becker, is now managing director of Arta Pay, and several former Art Money employees have joined the operation. Fields told ARTnews that the two businesses are separate, but argued that Arta has an advantage in its established technology platform and relationships with major art-market businesses.

According to recent reports, that existing network is central to Arta’s plans. Rather than building a financing business from scratch, the company is adding another service to a platform already used by galleries, auction houses, and collectors.

For now, Arta Pay is available to US citizens and residents, although they can use it to buy from participating sellers overseas. Applications take a few minutes, and most applicants receive a decision in real time following a soft credit check. The credit lines are issued by Lead Bank, with Arta handling the service.

Industry observers note that the question, of course, is whether giving collectors another way to spread out the cost of buying art will encourage them to buy more of it. For dealers who would rather spend their time selling paintings than chasing payments, the appeal is obvious.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual Hospices de Beaune charity wine auction in Burgundy, France, organized by Sotheby’s, generated €14.4 million ($15.8 million) on Sunday. It was the 166th edition of the the historic sale, and its top lot—known as the “Presidents’ Barrel”—was bought by Brazilian wine merchant Aloar Pereira Linoa for €770,000 ($848,732) in the room.

According to recent reports, just after the hammer came down, there was a surprise twist; the Faiveley family, one of Bergundy’s most important wine-making dynasties, pledged another €230,000 ($251,000), rounding up the total to a cool €1 million ($1.1 million).The donation brought the charitable total to a new record. Proceeds from the 228-liter Presidents’ Barrel (exempt from Sotheby’s buyer’s premium fees), which holds a Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru, will go to ARSLA and DEBRA, two charities supporting people with rare diseases. They are charcot disease and epidermolysis bullosa, otherwise known as “butterfly skin disease.”Each year, celebrities are enlisted to rev up the crowd and encourage bidding on the main barrel. This year saw comedy duo Éric Judor and Ramzy Bedia, alongside actress Aurelie Vandevoorde, temporarily take over at the rostrum. At one point, Judor promised the next bidder a minor role in his new movie, as the French trio had the room in raptures during the 18-minute bidding battle. “All you New Yorkers here… you’re willing to pay $20 for a hotdog but you won’t pay for this wine?” he joked.I’ve never seen people singing at an auction before, but at one point the entire crowd erupted into a standing performance of “Ban Bourguignon,” Burgundy’s unofficial anthem. Everyone raised their hands to shoulder level and twisted their wrists back and forth in rhythm, singing: “La, la, la, la, la, la….,” on repeat. Related Articles At Sotheby's $378.7 M. Doubleheader, Buyers Take Risks Again, Even as Bidding Drags Yayoi Kusama 'Infinity Net' Painting Sells for $15.1 M. at Sotheby's, Setting a Record.

Sources indicate that there were more than 600 people in the Halles de Beanue, a thatched-roof market hall just across from the Hôtel-Dieu de Beaune in the center of town. More than 350 registered participants from over 30 countries took part in the sale, with collectors also tuning in from a viewing event at Marcel in New York.“Like a work of art, every great Burgundy wine tells a story of place, time, and craftmanship,” Celian Ravel d’Estiennen Sotheby’s head of auction sales for wine in France, told ARTnews. “The 166th Hospices de Beaune sale celebrated precisely this heritage, as well as the generosity that has defined the event since 1859. The €1 million raised for the charities was a powerful testament to the emotional and cultural value of wine.”The Hospices de Beaune’s chief winemaker, Ludavine Griveau, was in tears as Vandevoorde brought the gavel down. “We can all be very proud of the work accomplished,” she noted.This year’s sale featured wines from the 2026 vintage, which was shaped by prolonged heat and dry conditions, including 53 days of heatwave. Harvesting began on August 15 in Pouilly-Fuissé, Beaune, and Meursault, the earliest start in the history of the Domaine des Hospices de Beaune, and wrapped up on August 24 in the Côte de Nuits. Yields were low, putting Griveau and her team under extra pressure, but the resulting wines were praised for their quality.In total, 48 barrels of 34 red wines and 86 barrels, including two half-barrels, of 18 white wines were sold, alongside 12 barrels and three half-barrels of eaux-de-vie. The auction ran over five hours. The average hammer price for a barrel of red and white wine was €31,156, marking the sixth consecutive year in which the figure has topped €30,000. Reds performed particularly well, with their average price rising 5 percent on last year to €28,931. White wines, meanwhile, saw something of a correction, according to Guillaume Koch, director and chairman of the board of the Hospices Civils de Beaune.

In a recent development, “The overall result of the sale is in line with our expectations, given the volumes offered this year,” Koch said. “We have seen the outstanding quality of the red wines duly recognised, while prices for the great white wines have undergone a correction.”Among the standout results were a barrel of Mazis-Chambertin Grand Cru, Cuvée Madeleine Collignon, which sold for €185,000, a record for the appellation; a barrel of Meursault Premier Cru Les Genevrières, Cuvée Philippe Le Bon, at €75,000; and a barrel of Pommard Premier Cru Les Epenots, Cuvée Dom Gobelet, at €40,000. Four of the five Pommard Village and Premier Cru cuvées offered also achieved fresh auction records.

Every November, the auction raises money for the Hospices Civils de Beaune, a charitable hospital network founded in the 15th century to care for the sick and poor. Proceeds from this year’s sale will also go towards a major program of digital modernisation, including a upcoming electronic patient record system and investment in laboratory and medical imaging equipment.The Hospices de Beaune auction took place alongside the town’s annual Trois Glorieuses, a three-day celebration of Burgundy’s wine and gastronomic heritage. The festivities brought together winemakers, négociants, collectors, and wine lovers for tastings, special dinners, and celebrations across Beaune and the surrounding vineyards, transforming the town into the center of the Burgundian wine world for the weekend. It’s pretty boozy, and lots of fun.Sotheby’s has been making a broader push into the global wine market, expanding its international reach through new specialist appointments, high-profile sales, and events designed to attract a younger generation of collectors. Its wine auction sales reached $127.5 million in 2025, up 12 percent year-on-year, with Burgundy accounting for 39 percent of the total.

Recent findings suggest that the house has held the Hospices de Beaune auction contract since 2021 and it runs until 2030. The house took it over from Christie’s, which ran it from 2005 to 2021.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Industry observers note that sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Sources indicate that stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Industry observers note that light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

According to recent reports, working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

Recent findings suggest that an occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

It has been revealed that diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

Recent findings suggest that the flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Industry observers note that once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

  • Released last week by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), the report stated that maintenance costs for the UNESCO-listed structure are expected to rise from £1.5 million to £2 million a week if no action is taken.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Image by Pandora Pictures courtesy of Shutterstock.

A government report has found that risks of a major fire at the Palace of Westminster are rising as health and safety incidents increase at the UK parliament building in London, amid continuing delays to its renovation.

Released last week by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), the report stated that maintenance costs for the UNESCO-listed structure are expected to rise from £1.5 million to £2 million a week if no action is taken. According to the latest report on the restoration, the overall cost of the renovation will rise by £420 million for each year the project is delayed.

Parliament voted in 2018 to vacate the Palace for restoration, however this has been delayed by ongoing disagreements about how fully the House of Commons and House of Lords should leave during the anticipated decades-long renovation.

“Political allergy” to updating the building.

According to Public Accounts Committee chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, current fire risks could result in “Notre Dame-like flames” at the parliament building, which in 2023 was reported by the committee to be at “constant risk of fire”.

“There has long been a political allergy to gripping the nettle that is R&R [repair and renovation],” Clifton-Brown stated.

“Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building’s roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life,” he continued.

“These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks which our committee identified three years ago.”.

Renovation strategy to be decided by 2030.

The report outlines four strategies for the renovation of the building laid out by the R&R Client Board, with one needing to be selected by parliament by 2030 for the programme to progress.

Sources indicate that two of these strategies have been recommended by the board in a bid to speed up the decision-making process. These are fully leaving the building, which is estimated to cost between £11.1 billion to £15.6 billion and take 19 to 24 years, and the partially vacating the building, which is estimated at £19.5 billion to £39.2 billion and could take up to 61 years.

Approving either of these recommendations would require parliamentary approval.

“All options ahead involve extremely high figures with very massive ranges,” Clifton-Brown stated.

“At a time of national fiscal constraint, we would expect the parliamentary authorities to examine these figures extremely carefully to see how they can be reduced before the vote.”.

The PAC’s report also found that there are areas that still need costing, including aspects like decommissioning, relocation of the building’s services, and the restoration of the medieval cloister court.

The cross-party committee has urged the clerks of both House of Commons and House of Lords to set out remaining cost estimates and provide a detailed schedule for the works.

“It is crucial that we preserve the palace as a symbol of our democracy,” the report said. “A failure to act would have serious consequences for taxpayers and future generations.”.

The renovation of the adjacent Elizabeth Tower was recently completed by architecture studio Purcell, and last year was awarded a RIBA London award.

#22251. Latest Update: Who Sat for Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait? A Fresh Catalog Essay Suggests It May Have Been the Artist

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (717 w)
📖 Baca

Latest Update: Who Sat for Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait? A Fresh Catalog Essay Suggests It May Have Been the Artist

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The catalog for the exhibition “Van Eyck: The Portraits” opening at London’s National Gallery on November 21, has reignited a long-standing debate about the identity of couple in the Early Netherlandish master’s mysterious Arnolfini Portrait (1434).
  • Sources indicate that in the painting, which is owned by the National Gallery and a centerpiece of the show, an elegantly dressed man and woman pose hand in hand in a private room.
  • In a recent development, the man and the woman are clearly husband and wife, though the work does not, as was once believed, depict a marriage ceremony.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The catalog for the exhibition “Van Eyck: The Portraits” opening at London’s National Gallery on November 21, has reignited a long-standing debate about the identity of couple in the Early Netherlandish master’s mysterious Arnolfini Portrait (1434). As reported in the Art Newspaper, one of the catalog’s essays suggests that the man in the painting, usually identified as a member of the Arnolfini family of Italian merchants, is in fact Jan van Eyck himself.

Sources indicate that in the painting, which is owned by the National Gallery and a centerpiece of the show, an elegantly dressed man and woman pose hand in hand in a private room. Every item in the chamber, including the couple’s fur-trimmed clothing, the oriental carpet on the floor, and even the orange resting on a windowsill—an expensive luxury at the time—signals understated wealth. Related Articles Clark Art Institute Unveils its Massive Aso Tavitian Gift, To Be Housed in a Brand-New Wing: 'Any Curator or Director's Dream' Why Is Hieronymus Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights So Vital?

In a recent development, the man and the woman are clearly husband and wife, though the work does not, as was once believed, depict a marriage ceremony. A 16th-century inventory of the holdings of Margaret of Austria, the painting’s owner at the time, identifies it as “Hernoul le Fin” or “Arnoult Fin,” which is widely interpreted by art historians as “Arnolfini.”.

According to recent reports, scholars have disagreed however, however, about which Arnolfini the man in the painting might be. Possible candidates are either Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (though recent discoveries suggest he was not married at the time the painting was made), or more likely his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini, who would have been in his late thirties in 1434.

Giovanni’s first wife Costanza Trenta died in 1433; thus, according to the National Gallery’s website, the woman is probably his second wife, whose identity is unknown. Alternatively, as art historian Margaret Koster and others have suggested, the painting may be a memorial piece.

It is also possible that the sitters were friends of Van Eyck’s. Reflected in the convex mirror behind them, two more men can be seen entering the room. Prominently written on the wall above the mirror is the inscription “Johannes de Eyck fuit hic. 1434” (“Jan van Eyck was here. 1434”), which is sometimes taken to mean that the men in the mirror are Van Eyck and his servant arriving for a visit.

But Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in one of the catalog’s essays, asserts instead that the subjects of the painting are Van Eyck and his wife Margaret. Kemperdick is a curator at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which owns several Van Eycks, including Portrait of a Man in a Red Chaperon (1390–1440/41) of the same man in the Arnolfini Portrait at an older age. He bases his theory on the inscription’s placement in the Arnolfini Portrait next to the male figure’s head, arguing that this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man.

Sources indicate that if true, Kemperdick’s theory would throw the identification of the subjects in other Van Eyck paintings into doubt. The National Gallery’s Portrait of a Man (1433), of a much older man than the man in the Arnolfini Portrait, is presently tentatively identified as a self-portrait, while the entry for the Berlin work—Kemperdick’s theory notwithstanding—still notes that it is presumed to be of Giovanni Arnolfini. (Both Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) and Portrait of a Man in a Red Chaperon (Giovanni Arnolfini?) are included in the exhibition, which brings together all nine of Van Eyck’s surviving portraits.).

For his part, Nicholas Flory, the exhibition’s co-curator along with Emma Capron, told the Art Newspaper that he found Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative.” He notes that the sitter in another work in the show from the Musea Brugge, definitively known to be of Margaret based on an inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.

German art historian Till-Holger Borchert, the former director of the Musea Brugge—concurs, finding the 16th-century inventory reference near conclusive proof that the painting is of an Arnolfini. But, he added, given how little is known about Van Eyck’s life, “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”.

Sources indicate that it’s not perfect. Because it has no light of its own, it needs a bright spot without harsh overhead glare, and images change slowly. There’s no app either, so everything runs through a website.

Industry observers note that it's also worth noting that Fraimic isn’t the only colour E Ink frame out there, as our guide to the best e-ink art frames highlights, and the SwitchBot AI Art Frame on that list creates AI images too. However the app you need for the latter pushes a $3.99 monthly subscription, while Fraimic gives you 100 free generations a year.

According to recent reports, tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just months after Yayoi Kusama‘s death, one of her paintings sold at Sotheby’s New York on Monday night for a hammer price of $12.5 million, or $15.1 million with fees, setting a new auction record for the artist.

In a recent development, the work sold after a brief bidding war between Evelyn Lin, chairman of modern and contemporary art, Asia, and Lisa Dennison, chairman of the Americas, both of whom were bidding on behalf of clients on the phone. Lin ultimately prevailed after 10 bids over the course of four minutes. The $12.5 million hammer price placed the work squarely within its presale estimate of $10 million to $15 million. Related Articles Sotheby's Hospices de Beaune Charity Wine Sale Nets $15.8 M. in France, with One Barrel Selling for Record $1.1 M. Sotheby's $180 M. Van Gogh Sale Faces Eleventh-Hour Nazi-Era Restitution Claim.

According to recent reports, no. 3P.B. (1960), is one of Kusama’s “Infinity Net” paintings, a series of large-scale monochrome abstractions in which the canvas is covered with thousands of looping brushstrokes. Kusama painted her first “Infinity Net” work in 1958, shortly after moving from Japan to Fresh York, which makes No. 3P.B. a rare early example of the form. The crimson canvas, which stands more than five feet tall, appeared in the Whitney Museum’s 1961 painting-focused annual exhibition, a precursor to the Whitney Biennial.

Industry observers note that about 10 lots later on Monday night, another painting from the series, Infinity Nets (OZEH), sold for a hammer price of $2.5 million, or $3.06 million with fees. That work, a white canvas measuring roughly 6½ by 8½ feet, is far more recent, dating to 2011.

Recent findings suggest that like Kusama’s “Infinity Mirror Rooms,” which are more popular on social media, the “Infinity Net” series deals with obsession and repetition. The series is often said to prefigure the Minimalism and Post-Minimalism of the 1960s and 1970s, and it made her name in a male-dominated art world. Reviewing the paintings for ARTnews in 1959, Donald Judd wrote, “The expression transcends the question of whether it is Oriental or American. Although it is something of both, certainly of such Americans as Rothko, Still and Newman, it is not at all a synthesis and is thoroughly independent.”.

Since Kusama died in August at 97, nearly 30 of her works have come to auction at Sotheby’s, Christie’s, and Phillips. The top results have been for two paintings of pumpkins, another of her signature motifs. At Sotheby’s Hong Kong in September, the 2010 painting Pumpkin (TWPOT) sold for HK$60.7 million, or about $7.74 million. The next day at Christie’s Hong Kong, the 2011 painting A-Pumpkin (YHP), which reveals a yellow pumpkin on a patterned black background, sold for HK$58.2 million, or about $7.43 million.

According to recent reports, besides No. 3P.B., 11 more Kusama works will go on the block this week. Five of them are “Infinity Net” paintings, but none is nearly as early or as highly valued.

Kusama’s previous auction record was set in 2022 at Phillips Newly introduced York by the 1959 painting Untitled (Nets), 1959, a white “Infinity Net” made a year before No. 3P.B. It sold for $10.5 million with fees.

#22248. Industry News: Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Industry News: Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

📅 09 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ah, creatine!
  • Industry observers note that creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells.
  • Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Industry observers note that creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Industry observers note that now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Sources indicate that does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

According to recent reports, some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

According to recent reports, beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Industry observers note that thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Sources indicate that furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

It has been revealed that creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#22247. At Sotheby’s $378.7 M. Doubleheader, Buyers Take Risks Again, Even as Bidding Drags

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1845 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Artnews ↗ Open Full Page

At Sotheby’s $378.7 M. Doubleheader, Buyers Take Risks Again, Even as Bidding Drags

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sotheby’s kicked off the November marquee sales with a doubleheader on Monday evening that generated $378.7 million across 74 lots.
  • The nearly three-hour marathon started strong with the dedicated sale from the collection of cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Baum sale was a lively affair from the start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sotheby’s kicked off the November marquee sales with a doubleheader on Monday evening that generated $378.7 million across 74 lots. The top-line results look solid, but a sluggish second half seemed to further illustrate the choosy mood among collectors right now.

The nearly three-hour marathon started strong with the dedicated sale from the collection of cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum. It was a white-glove result, with all 24 works sold for a hammer total of $90.9 million. With fees, the sale landed at $110 million, just a shade above the presale high estimate of $109 million. Related Articles Yayoi Kusama 'Infinity Net' Painting Sells for $15.1 M. at Sotheby's, Setting a Record Sotheby's Hospices de Beaune Charity Wine Sale Nets $15.8 M. in France, with One Barrel Selling for Record $1.1 M.

Recent findings suggest that the Baum sale was a lively affair from the start. After the first lot—Roy Lichtenstein’s 1983 cut-paper work Two Paintings: Sleeping Muse (Study)—sparked a four-minute contest among three specialists and a bidder in the room, CEO Charles Stewart strode over to Gareth Jones, the house’s chief marketing officer, and remarked of the $3.8 million total, “Well, that’s a good start.” Three lots later, a Lucio Fontana copper canvas with a glorious cut down the middle ignited another bidding war, the bids ricocheting among three bidders in the room. It hammered at $3.5 million, or $4.4 million with fees, well above the $3 million high estimate.

Oliver Barker, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, handled the proceedings with panache, making even a fairly ordinary stretch of bidding feel brisk. Amid the bidding for Lot 7, Andy Warhol’s 1984 painting The Scream (After Munch), he teased Jacqueline Wachter, chairwoman of private sales, for taking a bit too long with her phone bidder, asking whether she was “doing her shopping or doing her conversions.” Then he quipped to the audience, “Amazon is always open. As is Sotheby’s Dot Com.” It was a little sharp, perhaps, but it got a laugh and helped lighten the mood as the sale began to drag.

The crowded salesroom was a who’s who of the art trade: Dominique Lévy, Brett Gorvy, Amalia Dayan, David Schrader, Emmanuel Di Donna, Christophe Van de Weghe, and Gagosian Art Advisory’s Bernard Lagrange were just a few of the heavies in attendance.

In a recent development, in the end, six works hammered above their estimates and another 10 landed in range, with spirited bidding throughout, both in the room and on the phone. Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest led the sale at $19.3 million, followed by Mark Rothko’s Untitled at $17.7 million and Ed Ruscha’s Dimple at $11.6 million. The Baums had bought the Mitchell privately in 1986 for just $65,000, making its sale price nearly 300 times what they paid. The Rothko, which they acquired for $115,000 in 1983, brought more than 150 times its purchase price. Not bad for a few decades of collecting. The final lot in the sale, Mario Merz’s neon sculpture Iguana, sold well below its estimate, but that did little to dampen the enthusiasm, as the room erupted in applause.

The Now and Contemporary sale that followed was considerably less celebratory. Of the 53 lots originally offered, three were withdrawn before the sale, and another five went unsold: works by Kerry James Marshall, Ellsworth Kelly, Roy Lichtenstein, and Keith Haring, and, curiously, a Formula One race car. Tom Eddison, head of contemporary art at Sotheby’s London, who took over auctioneering duties for the sale, noted the car was a first for the auction house, and it required a lengthy preamble explaining that the sale was subject to the terms of service of RM Sotheby’s, the house’s classic-car affiliate. The car garnered a handful of bids but failed to reach its low estimate before Eddison declared it unsold. It may be some time before Sotheby’s tries that experiment again.

That’s not to say the results for the contemporary sale were lackluster. When all was said and done, the sale garnered a hammer total of $224.8 million. With fees, the total climbed to $268.8 million, within the presale aggregate estimate of $226.2 million to $323 million, and well above the equivalent sale in November 2025, which generated $178.5 million. Of course, we should note that last year’s sale followed the trove of works from the late cosmetics heir Leonard Lauder, which generated an eye-watering $527.5 million. Alas, not every season sees three Klimts hit the block.

Of the 45 lots that sold, a full 14 hammered above their presale estimates, and another 24 landed in range. Still, while there always seemed to be a handful of bidders for each sold lot, with Eddison darting his hands left, right, and center, most works hammered after only a minute or two.

It has been revealed that the most protracted bidding wars came somewhat early. A six-minute contest among four specialists for Jeff Koons’s 1991 sculpture Bob-Tail ended with contemporary art specialist Bame Fierro March winning the lot for a hammer price of $9 million. At $10.7 million with fees, that’s good for just over three times the high estimate. (Is Koons’s market trending back up, or do collectors just really like an adorable English sheepdog?) Seven lots later, Agnes Martin’s cream canvas Desert, from the collection of Lenore and Bernard Greenberg, sold after a six-minute duel between contemporary art specialist Alya Sama and Lisa Dennison, chairman of the Americas. Dennison won on a $9.2 million hammer bid, or $11.3 million with fees, comfortably above the $8 million high estimate. And Andy Warhol’s 1964–65 painting Flowers fetched $18.2 million with fees against a $10 million to $15 million estimate.

Mark the Warhol and Koons results as green shoots for a market that’s spent much of the past two years playing it safe. Neither artist has had the easiest time in the secondary market lately, which makes those results particularly interesting. Something to watch going forward, especially for Koons.

After the sale, Dennison pointed to the continued strength of early Martin paintings, which have been outperforming expectations for several seasons.

Recent findings suggest that art adviser Ed Dolman similarly found the night’s results encouraging. In a text message toward the end of the sale, he said, “The best works always do fine, [but] buyers were taking some risks again.”.

Dolman also pointed to the depth of bidding. While 29 of the 45 sold lots in the contemporary sale had guarantees—as did every work in the Baum sale—those guarantors were often outbid on Monday night. Buyers, it seemed, were willing to go a little further.

In a recent development, not that everything was suddenly flying off the walls. Lichtenstein’s Reflections on ‘Painter and Model,’ the top lot of the contemporary sale at $24.7 million with fees, came in well short of the high end of its $20 million to $30 million estimate. Willem de Kooning’s Water…Soft Banks of a Window (Untitled VIII) brought $20.3 million, just above its $20 million low estimate, while Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I made $17.1 million against a $15 million to $20 million estimate.

The buzziest result of the night was no doubt for Yayoi Kusama’s 1960 painting No. 3P.B., which hammered for $12.5 million after 10 bids spread across four minutes. With fees, the result came to $15.1 million, just above the $15 million high estimate, and good for a new record for the artist, who died in August. About 10 lots later, another of her “Infinity Nets” paintings, Infinity Nets (OZEH), sold for a hammer price of $2.5 million, or $3.1 million with fees, just a shade above the $3 million high estimate. That work, a white canvas measuring roughly 6½ by 8½ feet, is far more recent, dating to 2011. And if you missed out on those two Kusamas, have no fear: Another 10 works of hers will hit the block over the rest of marquee week. Five are from her long-running “Infinity Nets” series.

Yet, for all the strong prices, the second half of the contemporary sale was a slog. With Eddison at the rostrum, the pace slowed considerably. Bids were drawn out, pauses stretched on, and even works that eventually fetched impressive prices seemed to take an age to get there. A few market watchers wondered whether such a sluggish tempo might discourage bidders, particularly on works that didn’t have much competition to begin with. It was an odd contrast: a sale that sometimes felt as though it was struggling to find its rhythm, even as buyers were spending millions more than expected.

According to recent reports, to Nina Del Rio, an art adviser and auction house veteran, the results looked remarkably strong, particularly given the subdued energy in the second half of the sale. Still, she mentioned, there hasn’t been much evidence of a shift in the market. At least not a fundamental one. Buyers appear to be behaving much as they did in May, when the best works attracted serious money but enthusiasm for younger artists remained muted. A few years ago, the Now sale was where collectors went to get their hands on artists whose waiting lists seemed impossible to crack. That sense of urgency has largely disappeared.

What collectors do seem willing to pay for is scarcity. Del Rio pointed to the modern masterpieces coming up later in the week, the sort of works that rarely appear at auction and may not come around again for decades. Among them is Wednesday’s sale of the Blaquier Collection, a group of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist masterpieces remarked to be worth around $450 million, and a $180 million Van Gogh suddenly subject to a last-minute restitution claim.

Recent findings suggest that dennison warned against reading too much into a single evening. Given the current mood, starting the week with contemporary art rather than a mix of modern and contemporary masterpieces makes it harder to judge the market as a whole. And while works in the $10 million to $20 million range performed well, the sale lacked the $30 million, $40 million, and $50 million trophies that drive enthusiasm across the whole week.

It has been revealed that as for that Formula One car, Dennison said the result left her scratching her head. The last bid offered, $3.9 million, was just under the $4 million low estimate. Did the interested buyer really think the $100,000 gap was too wide to bridge?

Industry observers note that there is a risk to putting something unexpected into a contemporary art sale. But, as Dennison pointed out, sometimes it works, as when Christie’s sold the Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton “Stan” during its 20th Century Evening Sale in 2020 for $31.8 million, nearly quadruple the high estimate.

According to recent reports, sotheby’s shouldn’t give up on the idea. There’s something appealing about an evening sale that doesn’t draw a firm boundary around paintings and sculptures. Not every experiment works the first time, or even the second. And if the object is truly one-of-a-kind, buyers are ready to shell out the cash.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • RooMoo transformed a five-level former sales office into the Cloudhaus Hotel, retaining the building’s original structure while incorporating materials collected from the surrounding landscape and nearby villages.
  • Located at an altitude of 1,200 metres on the mountain’s northern slope, the building has a white-rendered facade punctuated by eight projecting white frames that extend vertically across its elevations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Wen Studio.

Concrete drill cores, discarded bricks and timber salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins have been repurposed for a 24-room retreat by Chinese studio RooMoo on Jinfo Mountain in Chongqing, China.

RooMoo transformed a five-level former sales office into the Cloudhaus Hotel, retaining the building’s original structure while incorporating materials collected from the surrounding landscape and nearby villages.

Located at an altitude of 1,200 metres on the mountain’s northern slope, the building has a white-rendered facade punctuated by eight projecting white frames that extend vertically across its elevations.

Bamboo panels and stone slabs fill sections between the frames, while timber detailing and sloping tiled roofs reference traditional buildings in the region.

Rather than using newly introduced materials, RooMoo visited local abandoned wooden cabins and furniture workshops to identify resources that could be reused. The studio ended up using timber from the cabins for the project.

“Instead of relying solely on research, we planned most of our conceptual design time to explore the mountains for locally available materials and resources to respect the local environment,” the studio mentioned.

Among the most unusual interventions are walls made from concrete cores extracted during structural renovations, which have been stacked vertically and separated by dark metal supports.

Demolished red bricks were reused in the restaurant, while discarded bamboo scaffolding treads were cut into strips and transformed into ceiling panels and outdoor paving.

The restaurant occupies an expanded podium at the building’s lower level, with indoor dining areas leading towards outdoor terraces.

Its interiors combine stone walls, timber furniture and woven seating, while reclaimed bricks and bamboo offcuts feature in the finishes.

Visitors enter the hotel via the reception on the building’s uppermost floor, which is accessed from an entrance courtyard and connecting bridge.

A timber reception desk sits in front of a wall covered in bamboo panels, woven surfaces and discarded bamboo-shoot shells, which had been harvested locally in the mountains.

Above the lobby, an exposed pitched roof was lined with bamboo and supported by substantial timber beams.

A large woven bamboo installation hangs over the lounge, where black sofas and tan leather chairs were arranged beside full-height glazing overlooking the forested mountains.

Guestrooms were arranged in a fan-shaped layout facing the mountain landscape.

The hotel offers several room types, including courtyard rooms, suites and standard king rooms, with interiors featuring earthy colours, salvaged timber and locally made furniture.

Founded in Shanghai in 2017 by Tao Zhang, Ray Zhang and Marine Bois, RooMoo works across hospitality, restaurant, commercial, office and residential projects.

Other recent interior projects in China include a Linehouse-designed hotel with an industrial feel and a Shanghai tea shop that draws on Rockbund’s historic buildings.

Photography by Wen Studio.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artsy and Artnet have another deal: The two art-market platforms unveiled the acquisition of First Thursday, a London-based startup that uses artificial intelligence to help galleries keep track of collectors, manage relationships, and, ideally, sell more art.
  • The purchase comes seven months after Artsy and Artnet joined forces under Beowolff Capital, the investment firm founded by Andrew Wolff.
  • Industry observers note that the latest deal, whose financial terms weren’t disclosed, is a little less controversial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artsy and Artnet have another deal: The two art-market platforms unveiled the acquisition of First Thursday, a London-based startup that uses artificial intelligence to help galleries keep track of collectors, manage relationships, and, ideally, sell more art.

The purchase comes seven months after Artsy and Artnet joined forces under Beowolff Capital, the investment firm founded by Andrew Wolff. And just last week, Artnet announced a partnership with Kalshi, the prediction-market platform that allows customers to bet on auction results, prompting a rather unenthusiastic response from parts of the art world. Related Articles Investor Says Artnet Layoffs Were Necessary for 'Financial Strength' Artnet Makes Significant Layoffs Following Consolidation with Artsy.

Industry observers note that the latest deal, whose financial terms weren’t disclosed, is a little less controversial. It also gives a clearer picture of what the combined manufacturer is trying to build: a single system that galleries can use to manage almost every part of their businesses.

Founded in 2023 by Callum Hale-Thomson, First Thursday specializes in what it calls “collector intelligence.” In practice, that means gathering years of emails, sales records, inquiries, and notes into one searchable place, then using AI to help dealers figure out which collectors might be interested in a particular work.

It has been revealed that hale-Thomson, whose parents are both artists, told ARTnews that the idea came to him after he spent six months working inside London galleries, effectively serving as their IT guy and watching how they operated. He found that many were sitting on years of valuable information without an easy way to use it.

According to recent reports, “You’re sitting on an unbelievable trove of information,” he mentioned, describing the emails, notebooks, and other records galleries accumulate over time. The problem was finding anything useful when it was needed.

It has been revealed that first Thursday’s existing software helps with that. At an art fair, for example, a dealer can scan a visitor’s business card, record which painting caught their eye, and send a follow-up email directly from thier phone. The system can also bring together past correspondence and publicly available information about collectors, helping galleries identify potential buyers they might otherwise have overlooked.

Recent findings suggest that under the upcoming ownership, Hale-Thomson and his team will help develop a broader gallery-management platform, scheduled to launch for select Artsy and Artnet partners in early 2027. It will combine collector records with inventory management, sales tools, invoicing, marketing, and online viewing rooms. Galleries will also be able to publish works to Artsy and Artnet directly from the system.

The initial focus will be smaller galleries, which often lack the money or staff to maintain sophisticated software.

Alex Forbes, who oversees global partnerships for Artsy and Artnet, told ARTnews that the smallest gallery partners will be able to use the core system without paying more than they already do for their Artsy subscriptions.

Sources indicate that larger galleries will be able to purchase additional features and access for bigger teams. Exact pricing will be confirmed when the platform debuts.

“We want it to be the easiest to start out with for a small gallery,” Forbes said, while also making it useful for businesses with more complicated operations.

The move takes Artsy and Artnet further into a competitive market for gallery software, where established companies such as Artlogic already offer inventory and business-management tools. Last year, Artlogic merged with ArtCloud, another sign of consolidation in the art-tech business. (Artsy is already integrated with Artlogic and Artcloud, which, according to an Artsy spokesperson, the tech giant will continue to support.).

Industry observers note that forbes acknowledged that galleries have different needs and that no single product will necessarily suit everyone. But he said the broader initiative is to connect the tech giant’s existing marketplaces and pricing data with the software that galleries use to run their businesses.

Industry observers note that one potentially sensitive question is what happens to all that collector information. Artsy and Artnet say galleries will retain control of their data, which will remain private unless they choose to share it with the platforms.

For Hale-Thomson, who will remain with the business, the opportunity is to bring more sophisticated tools to galleries that haven’t traditionally been able to afford them.

Sources indicate that and for Artsy and Artnet, the acquisition marks another step toward becoming something considerably bigger than two websites where people look at art, check prices, and occasionally buy something. Increasingly, they want to provide the software that keeps the business running.
