Latest Update: Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone.
  • It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body.
  • Recent findings suggest that retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Recent findings suggest that retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

According to recent reports, but retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next substantial thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

In a recent development, retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”.

The medication is at the moment in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide customers lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In a recent development, in fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

Recent findings suggest that “Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”.

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

According to recent reports, “People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”.

Industry observers note that that includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he states.

But, with all medications, Dr. Ali states it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle blueprint focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel claims. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

In a recent development, if you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more crucial, he points out.

Breaking: Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design claims innovation lead

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers.
  • According to recent reports, “I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon.
  • Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Nike.

According to recent reports, sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

According to recent reports, “I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”.

Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” remarked McCartney.

“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”.

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

“At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” remarked McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”.

It has been revealed that “If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”.

According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

In a recent development, “It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” stated McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”.

“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

Sources indicate that “So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “.

Industry observers note that while the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

Industry observers note that “There’ll be a few modifications,” he stated. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.

“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”.

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “important part of the design and important part of this platform”.

It has been revealed that the midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.

In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

Sources indicate that “There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”.

According to recent reports, “We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” said McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”.

Photography courtesy of Nike.

The newest class of the WNBA is already stepping into the spotlight. Monday’s draft night delivered all the energy you’d expect from a league entering a pivotal chapter. With a newly introduced collective bargaining agreement reshaping conversations around players’ salaries, benefits, and long-term investment, the future of the WNBA is looking bigger, better, and brighter.

According to recent reports, this year’s top picks come in with stacked resumes, impressive tournament runs, championship wins, and star power already on the rise. Game day mantra: “Keep going and trust in your work.”.

College: University of California, Los Angeles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump unveiled the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

Sources indicate that “This is a special structure,” Trump noted on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”.

According to recent reports, it claims everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8.

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.

Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

Architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.

“[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.

It has been revealed that the ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s West Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.

It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history.

In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion said it was “likely unlawful”.

Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.

The administration has also floated intends to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

#22145. Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

📅 15 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (886 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation.
  • The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected.
  • “These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But new research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

“These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

In a recent development, the research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

It has been revealed that the researchers discovered that while participants said they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

Sources indicate that “We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”.

Ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh claims. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”.

In a recent development, people are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

As a result, Dr. Gallagher claims she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”.

These chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

“Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen notes. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Sources indicate that loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a significant impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen claims.

Recent findings suggest that over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan says. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

Sources indicate that of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan notes. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”.

Sources indicate that ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she notes. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2484 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year winner named

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2484 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.
  • The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.
  • Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.

The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.

V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

The master jury cited the project as a “sophisticated wayfinding scheme that demonstrates how signage can do far more than direct: it can define identity, shape experience and establish a sense of place”.

The judges praised the design for its “clarity, confidence and restraint, seamlessly guiding visitors through the V&A East Storehouse while adding to the character of the building”.

V&A East Storehouse was up against designs that included a constellation of gloopy-looking polished resin lights, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van and a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:.

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse.

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” mentioned the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”.

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects.

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial.

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

Recent findings suggest that “What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges mentioned. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design.

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

Recent findings suggest that its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” said the master jury.

“The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”.

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée.

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship.

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

First, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

“Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”.

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas.

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.

It has been revealed that baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes consumers away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” remarked the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”.

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii.

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges remarked.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”.

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht.

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline.

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic.

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic tech giant, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” said the judges.

According to recent reports, “The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”.

Looking ahead, the judges stated “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”.

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko.

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this newly introduced material adds value to the waste.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

“Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they stated. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”.

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition.

Recent findings suggest that designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” said the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal.

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries.

Recent findings suggest that the four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

Sources indicate that “This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”.

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes.

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered.

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

“This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges stated. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”.

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health.

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions.

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

“This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges said. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”.

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again.

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

Recent findings suggest that “This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”.

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio.

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete.

The project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” remarked the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”.

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front.

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology company Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete.

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

“As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”.

How to Use Jojoba Oil for Hair: Expert Tips for Stunning Results

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.
  • The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds.
  • Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

Industry observers note that “Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” indicates Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo says it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

While its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo claims.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”.

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily quickly after washing,” Macedo notes, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”.

She says adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo indicates she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:.

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo claims you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she says can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Sources indicate that kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

It has been revealed that macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”.

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

Kobets says that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Recent findings suggest that do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, Azerbaijan, rises in fluid curves and folds in the midst of a wide clearing in the city's gridded forest of urban blocks. The striking structure, completed in 2013 by Zaha Hadid Architects, acts as a primary venue for the country's cultural programs. Its curvaceous form sits in contrast to its rectilinear surroundings, marking its importance. The carefully curated curves epitomize a constant ambition in the studio's work–to dissolve the distinction between the horizontal and the vertical, between inside and outside, and between landscape and building. Needless to say, its complexity marks it as a feat of construction as well as of architecture. As Zaha Hadid Architects note, "Advanced computing allowed for the continuous control and communication of these complexities among the numerous project participants." Indeed, it is computing that made the building of the center possible, as well as other projects by the studio. As architecture becomes increasingly entangled with the digital realm, one can even ask if this is a triumph of the discipline or that of computation.

Zaha Hadid's built projects may have been propelled by computational development, but her early unbuilt projects were characterized by geometric hand-painted proposals that blended the intervention with its context. This is an example of architecture's relationship with technology, which is as old as the profession itself, at times exhibiting a slow adoption, and at times being transformed. When Imhotep pioneered stone construction in Saqqara, Egypt, the pillars were carved to resemble the reeded construction, while the triglyphs on the entablature of the Doric Order in Greek architecture were a feature of the timber construction that preceded it. Newly introduced construction technology was adopted piecemeal, while retaining the familiarity of the old.

Industry observers note that although numbers and geometry are fundamental in building, developments in mathematics gradually entered architecture and construction also. In Renaissance Europe, studies in proportions and mensuration became guiding principles in architectural composition. In the Islamic world, complex mathematical geometry and tessellating forms were adopted. The advent of engineering during the Industrial Revolution gave mathematics in building upcoming importance. The knowledge that was used to power the steam engine and construct the railways was applied to the great roofs of the train stations, bringing engineering to buildings. The relationship between architecture and engineering is key, as computation would later also reach the realm of architecture through engineering.

At the time of writing, two recent books explore the relationship between architecture and computation. The Evolution of Computation in Architecture by Bradley Bell and Michael Fox, published in 2024, presents an overview of the pioneers who led the paradigm shift in architecture through computation. A year earlier, Beyond Digital: Design and Automation at the End of Modernity by Mario Carpo was published, reviewing the history that led to the role of computation today, but also identifying trends away from standardization and mass production to bespoke manufacture and specificity.

The Evolution of Computation in Architecture by Bradley Bell and Michael Fox, published in 2024, presents an overview of the pioneers who led the paradigm shift in architecture through computation. A year earlier, Beyond Digital: Design and Automation at the End of Modernity by Mario Carpo was published, reviewing the history that led to the role of computation today, but also identifying trends away from standardization and mass production to bespoke manufacture and specificity.

Bell and Fox detail the cycle through which a upcoming technology enters a discipline in seven steps. This starts with context, where there is a coalescence of both technological and socioeconomic forces, followed by several stages of pioneering and innovation, culminating in a new paradigm of operation. An example of a full cycle would be the use of CAD in architecture, while a yet-incomplete cycle example is that of artificial intelligence.

Bell and Fox detail the cycle through which a newly introduced technology enters a discipline in seven steps. This starts with context, where there is a coalescence of both technological and socioeconomic forces, followed by several stages of pioneering and innovation, culminating in a new paradigm of operation. An example of a full cycle would be the use of CAD in architecture, while a yet-incomplete cycle example is that of artificial intelligence.

Industry observers note that it is fair to say that the relationship between architecture and computing began in the 1960s. After the invention of electronic transistors and the exponential growth of computing power since the Second World War, mainframe computers in large institutions became the frontier of this latest technology. Alongside this were genuine attempts at bringing architecture and computing together, including visionary speculation well beyond the computing power of the time. The Fun Palace by Cedric Price and Joan Littlewood was one such example, designed as a framework with multiple and continuously changing functions that suit the users' needs. Through feedback and computation, this adaptation can be automated such that the building changes and reorganizes itself.

After the invention of electronic transistors and the exponential growth of computing power since the Second World War, mainframe computers in large institutions became the frontier of this newly introduced technology. Alongside this were genuine attempts at bringing architecture and computing together, including visionary speculation well beyond the computing power of the time. The Fun Palace by Cedric Price and Joan Littlewood was one such example, designed as a framework with multiple and continuously changing functions that suit the users' needs. Through feedback and computation, this adaptation can be automated such that the building changes and reorganizes itself.

Perhaps the most significant attempt came from Nicholas Negroponte's Architecture Machine Group, a lab and think-tank established in 1967 at MIT to study human-computer relations. It included the creation of a computer program that would effectively replicate the job of an architect, produced by feeding the machine a vast collection of architectural rules that would inform the algorithms. Partly due to the processing power available at the time, and partly due to the rule-based approach, the program was not a success, and many of its failures were captured in Negroponte's eponymous book, The Architecture Machine, published in 1970.

Partly due to the processing power available at the time, and partly due to the rule-based approach, the program was not a success, and many of its failures were captured in Negroponte's eponymous book, The Architecture Machine, published in 1970.

The next decade or two saw computation take a different direction. Devices became smaller and cheaper, and therefore more accessible, culminating in the home computer. Instead of the focus on computing power and ever more complex expectations, communication and representation came to the fore. Computer-Aided Design (CAD) was a term coined in the 1950s and largely used in mechanical engineering, but in the 80s and 90s the technology gradually crept into architectural practice. Imagery and graphics, which were too heavy for 1960s processors, could later be handled by the smaller personal computers in architecture firms.

Industry observers note that thus, computing became a method for architectural firms to gain efficiency and improve communication. But when did computing begin to take an active role in design, and not just act as a graphical tool? Enter Frank Gehry and the fish. The 'Peix' sculpture (meaning 'fish' in Catalan) was constructed on the Barcelona waterfront for the 1992 Olympic Games. After it was first conceived, managing its structural behavior and construction method proved impossible without the use of CATIA, a software package used by the aeronautics industry and famously used to design the Boeing 777 aircraft. Not long after, the Guggenheim in Bilbao was built in 1997, firmly announcing the arrival of computation in the design of buildings.

The 1990s saw the beginning of a second wave of excitement with computation in architecture. Programs originally created for other disciplines, like Rhino, entered the field. The term 'parametricism' was often used by Patrik Schumacher of Zaha Hadid Architects, describing computer-generated elements with the ability to adapt and easily integrate into CAD-CAM production. Elsewhere, software was used for data mapping, including GIS, and for highly sophisticated environmental modelling, such as with Ecotect.

Alongside these real-world applications, theoretical speculation also returned. There was Greg Lynn's Embryonic House, a blob of splines which could be manipulated to produce various permutations of forms. In design, the Computational Chair by Philippe Morel celebrated the 'voxel' (volumetric pixel), produced by a computer program that generated thousands of potential forms, but only 25 were chosen for production. Digital Grotesque I by Michael Hansmeyer and Benjamin Dillenburger was a speculative narrative space installation, with no function, but that explored the potential of digital technologies. Similarly, artist Philip Beesley created interactive environments combining 'synthetic biology, artificial intelligence, mechanics, sound, light, and filtering systems'. Architect Hernan Diaz Alonso took things further, creating surreal digital spaces that only existed in digital space. This was the digital for the sake of the digital.

The question then becomes: is this a triumph of architecture entering latest realms, or of computation overwhelming the discipline? Should architects think more like programmers, imagining adaptable digital creatures that would eventually become our dwellings? With the speed of development in artificial intelligence, will buildings simply be vibe-coded into existence? Time will tell. What is certain, however, is that movements in any direction always have a reaction. MP3 and streaming have not killed vinyl. Additionally, digital systems have been deployed to democratize architecture and improve its affordability. The WikiHouse project, for example, aims to make well-designed net-zero homes available to the wider public. The Block Research Group at ETH Zurich aims to refine structures so they use the least material, using digital tools. The Heydar Aliyev Center may be a visually breathtaking feat of digital design. But it is one stepping stone on the arc of digital history.

#22141. Tech Report: Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

📅 15 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (885 w)

Tech Report: Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity.
  • Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.
  • At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity. But in reality, they’re both effective cardio options that challenge your body in distinct ways—from the muscles you recruit to the impact on your joints. Both workouts can boost your heart health, build endurance, and leave you seriously sweaty, but they place different demands on your body, according to Gab Reznik, CPT and Tone House coach. The question isn’t which is better across the board—it’s which is better for you depending on your goals.

Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.

At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.

“Any movement is better than no movement at all—whether that’s incline walking or running,” Reznik tells SELF. “They’re both effective at increasing blood flow, elevating heart rate, and improving overall aerobic capacity.” That means stronger heart and lung function over time—which are key markers of long-term health.

They also both demand muscular effort. Running requires you to generate power with every stride, while incline walking emphasizes controlled, deliberate steps against gravity (thanks to the incline). “Over time, the repetitive impact and loading can help strengthen joints and support long-term durability when done properly,” Reznik says.

While they may look similar on the surface, incline walking and running are different in two major ways: how hard they push your body, and how much stress they place on your joints.

Running is the higher-impact option. With each stride, your joints absorb roughly two to three times your body weight. That added force typically translates to higher intensity—and more calories burned per hour, Reznik explains.

Incline walking, on the other hand, keeps one foot on the ground at all times, reducing overall joint load. “Incline walking is more sustainable for longer durations,” Reznik states. “At the same fitness level, someone will typically be able to maintain an incline walk longer than a run due to the lower per-step demand.”.

It’s easy to think of incline walking as purely cardio—but that’s only part of its benefits.

“Incline walking can absolutely build strength, just not in the same way as lifting weights,” Reznik indicates. Instead of maximizing muscle growth by picking up heavy weights, incline walking improves muscular endurance, particularly in the lower body (think: glutes, hamstrings, and calves).

The steeper the incline, the greater the challenge. And if you want to level up even more, try adding external load, like a weighted vest, Reznik suggests. “It can increase the strength stimulus without significantly increasing joint impact.”.

Recent findings suggest that still, it’s crucial to keep your expectations realistic. If your goal is to build maximal strength or increase muscle size, traditional strength training should still be your primary focus.

One of the biggest misconceptions about incline walking is that it’s somehow inferior to running. Reznik is quick to shut that down.

“Walking isn’t less effective—it’s simply a different type of stimulus,” she says.

In a recent development, in fact, incline walking can be deceptively tough. Imagine this: a 15% incline at 3 mph for 30 minutes, without holding onto the treadmill. “That’s extremely challenging—even for a trained runner,” Reznik says.

In a recent development, both workouts can improve cardiovascular fitness and support fat loss when programmed appropriately. The key is understanding that “effective” doesn’t mean “hardest”—it means the movement is aligned with your fitness goals.

If you’re aiming to maximize calorie burn in a shorter amount of time or really test your cardiovascular endurance, running may be the more efficient choice, Reznik states. Its higher intensity makes it ideal for pushing your limits.

In a recent development, but if you’re looking to reduce joint stress while still building aerobic fitness (and even some muscular endurance), incline walking may be the smarter pick. “If you treat them as complementary, you can unlock a higher level of performance and longevity,” Reznik states.

Deciding between incline walking and running ultimately comes down to three factors: your goals, your current fitness level, and what you actually enjoy enough to stick with.

Beginners might start with a light jog at a conversational pace or a slight incline (around 2% to 3%) at a comfortable walking speed, Reznik suggests. From there, it’s crucial to progress either the speed or incline, but not both at once.

According to recent reports, “Incline walking isn’t the ‘easy’ option—it’s the smart option when used correctly,” Reznik states. “Running isn’t the ‘better’ option—it’s the specific option when it aligns with your goals.”.

A well-rounded routine might include both: running for higher-intensity days when you want to challenge your cardio limits, and incline walking for longer, lower-impact sessions that still deliver a serious burn.

According to recent reports, ultimately, there’s no clear winner between incline walking and running because they aren’t rivals. Both movements can be tools for improving heart health, building endurance and strengthening key muscle groups. The better workout is the one that helps you move consistently and safely. And in many cases, the smartest approach isn’t choosing between them—it’s using both.

Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year unveiled

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An old sailor’s home that pays homage to its nautical heritage has won Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year following the announcement of all 14 interiors category winners at a party in London.
  • The 14 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme are located in 10 different countries, including Australia, China, Czech Republic, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Ukraine.
  • La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects won the interiors project of the year award, sponsored by Gaggenau.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An old sailor’s home that pays homage to its nautical heritage has won Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year following the announcement of all 14 interiors category winners at a party in London.

The 14 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme are located in 10 different countries, including Australia, China, Czech Republic, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Ukraine.

La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects won the interiors project of the year award, sponsored by Gaggenau. It was also named residential interior (small) project of the year.

“This was probably the boldest and most well-executed project we saw,” noted the judges.

“They kept everything that was already there and made a much more interesting place,” adding that, “it’s very well-thought-out in terms of how space has been used.”.

La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners, including a restaurant that features “direct and unrefined” materials to create tactile interior in Canada, a pink stepped-facade-fronted commercial building and interiors in Mexico and a boutique that recalls a traditional yurt in Kazakhstan.

A boutique hotel in Bali focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture and a warehouse into a workspace divided by glass partitions and filled with design classics, including an entire Jean Prouvé house were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning interiors projects below:.

Interiors project of the year and residential interior (small) of the year: La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects.

The Spanish practice renovated the home in Mataro, Spain, which belonged to a sailor in the 19th century, updating its interiors to suit the lifestyle of his descendant, who lives there now.

There was no discussion – this was the winner.

The project saw the renovation of three spaces: the entrance hall, the dining room and the living area. The judges praised the project’s bold approach, noting there was no deliberation over its winning credentials: “There was no discussion – this was the winner.”.

“It’s super unusual,” they continued, “and we liked to see an intervention in a very historical space where they decided to not play it safe.”.

Residential interior (large) of the year: Garden Home by Gisbert Pöppler.

Local studio Gisbert Pöppler won residential interior (large) of the year for its renovation of a 1920s villa in Ruhr, Germany.

For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior.

The interior design features a bold colour scheme and artisanal details that reflect its association with the Deutscher Werkbund movement, which caught the judges’ eyes.

“For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior,” they said.

“It has character and doesn’t play it safe,” they continued.

Restaurant interior of the year: Jeju by &Daughters.

Canadian studio &Daughters won restaurant interior of the year for Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver, Canada.

This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element.

A rich material palette of basalt, cork, concrete, thatch and wood characterises the restaurant interior, which nods to traditional touches in its contemporary design.

“This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element,” the master jury noted. “It’s contemporary and still a bit traditional. There’s also a cultural influence that’s being used well and isn’t just there for decoration.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Bar and cafe interior of the year: Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design.

Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design in Xi’an, China, won bar and cafe interior of the year, sponsored by Programa.

There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it.

Located inside the Beilin Museum, the cafe’s interior aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty and used a minimal intervention renovation strategy with every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

“This project is latest and modern, but still connected to the past,” the judges said.

“There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it.”.

“The architect has taken symbolic elements and simplified them, which makes it feel quite fresh.”.

Hotel and short-stay interior of the year: Moon Gang by YSG Studio.

Australian studio YSG won hotel and short-stay interior of the year for its conversion of a former private vacation residence into a boutique hotel in Bali, Indonesia.

There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit.

Focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture, Moon Gang Bali hotel is located among the rice fields on the northern outskirts of Ubud and includes five interconnected suites, outdoor terraces and a lounge surrounding a central courtyard.

YSG was influenced by Indonesian and Japanese design for the hotel’s spaces, which feature bamboo and timber structures and lava stone tiling.

“There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit,” commended the master jury.

Workplace interior (small) of the year: Rosadoce by Reims 502.

Rosadoce by Reims 502 in Querétaro, Mexico won workplace interior (small) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior.

Featuring a stepped facade, the commercial building’s pink characterises the warm feel of the interior, being used throughout the workplace with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone.

“This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior,” noted the master jury.

“We like how they connected the interior and exterior design,” they continued, “it’s an adaptable and very sophisticated design.”.

Workplace interior (large) of the year: Not A Hotel Office by Not A Hotel.

Not a Hotel’s own office in Tokyo, Japan won workplace interior (large) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic.

The Japanese hospitality company’s in-house architecture team turned a 1967 warehouse into a workspace featuring a brutalist design divided by glass partitions and a spacious interior with seven-metre-tall ceilings.

“We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic,” said the judges.

“It really makes coming to the office feel like a dip back into the culture.”.

Retail interior (small) of the year: Gunia Project Showroom by Temp Project.

Local studio Temp Project won retail interior (small) of the year for its lifestyle store in Kyiv, Ukraine.

The mix between the old and latest is very interesting.

Modern materials, including mirrors and tiled surfaces, were used to complement the building’s original ornate interior for brand Gunia Project, which occupies the ground floor of a late 19th-century building located on a historic street near Kyiv’s Golden Gate.

“The mix between the old and new is very interesting,” said the judges.

“It must have been a constraining space to work in,” they observed, “but the end result feels very carefully edited and sophisticated.”.

Retail interior (large) of the year: Messa House by Up2date.

Up2date Architects won retail interior (large) of the year for the minimalist Messa House store in Almaty, Kazakhstan.

Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect.

Commissioned for womenswear brand Messa, the 350-square-metre store was designed to reimagine the form of a Kazakh yurt, with breakout areas and an on-site cafe.

“Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect,” praised the master jury.

The judges also commended “the contrast between the glossy tiles, wall and furniture”.

“It’s like a small architectural world inside the space,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Leisure and wellness interior of the year: Unravel by Atelier Write.

Japanese studio Atelier Write won the leisure and wellness interior of the year for its hair salon project in Tokyo, Japan.

This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there.

Named Unravel, the project transformed a warehouse with statement features such as suspending mirrors, shelves and curtains from a series of industrial rails that allow the entire space to be reconfigured.

“This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there,” remarked the judges.

“It’s an innovative, moveable space and the movement has purpose; it’s not just a gimmick.”.

Exhibition design (interior) of the year: Life Behind the Walls by B² Architecture.

B2 Architecture won exhibition design (interior) of the year for its Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, Czech Republic.

They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a new way.

Using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea, the 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

“In this project, the colours black, white and red are used really well in a graphical way,” remarked the master jury.

The judges also noted its material sensitivity, noting how surprising “the designers use soft materials to create emotions,” adding that “there’s a contrast between the technology and the use of textiles”.

“They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a new way,” they added.

Kitchen interior of the year: Pine Island Cottage by Thom Fougere Studio & Bureau Tempo.

Canadian studios Bureau Tempo and Thom Fougere won kitchen interior of the year for Pine Island Cottage in Ontario, Canada.

You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them.

The getaway retreat’s materials are informed by the rocky surroundings of the host island in Ontario’s Georgian Bay.

“This kitchen is very functional and well laid out, but it’s also super beautiful and we like that they used local materials,” noted the master jury.

“You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them.”.

Bathroom interior of the year: Lumeah by Pepper & Well.

Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well won bathroom interior of the year for Lumeah in Macedon, Australia.

We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass.

The studio took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing the latest en-suite within one of the most intact examples of residential work by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

“We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass,” mentioned the judges.

“The studio did a good job of creating a contemporary interior in a historic building, and we enjoyed how the bathroom feels like it continues out into the garden.”.

Sustainable interior of the year: Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo Design Studio.

Chinese studio RooMoo won sustainable interior of the year for Cloudhaus Hotel in Chongqing, China.

This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done.

RooMoo transformed a five-level former sales office into the Cloudhaus Hotel, retaining the building’s original structure while incorporating materials collected from the surrounding landscape and nearby villages.

Concrete drill cores, discarded bricks and timber salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins were repurposed for the 24-room retreat for its renovation, which the judges noted for being well-documented.

“This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done,” the master jury said.

“They took a dark, concrete space and turned it into a warm interior through the use of wood, while keeping a lot of the existing materials,” they continued.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

💡 Key Takeaways
